desc_declarative_claude:
The module Rec9 is a small model-checking demonstration that verifies a recursive set-cardinality function against TLA+'s built-in `Cardinality` operator.

The module defines a constant upper bound `MAX_NUM` equal to 5 and a number domain `NUMS` equal to `1..5`. Two variables are used: `set`, a subset of `NUMS`, and `size`, an integer tracking the computed cardinality. The recursive function `Card` is defined over all subsets of `NUMS`: it returns 0 for the empty set and otherwise picks an arbitrary element, removes it, and adds 1 to the recursive result. The module notes that this definition, while elegant, forces construction of the full powerset of `NUMS` and is at least double-exponential in cost.

The initial state sets `set` to the empty set and `size` to 0. Each step nondeterministically picks some element `i` from `NUMS`, adds it to `set`, and updates `size` by applying `Card` to the new set. The invariant `Inv` asserts that `size` always equals `Cardinality(set)`, confirming that the hand-written recursive `Card` function produces the same result as the built-in operator across all reachable states.
desc_intent:
Specify a system that incrementally builds a finite set drawn from a fixed finite universe and maintains a separate numeric value that always equals the set's cardinality. The system should allow adding individual elements from the universe to the set one at a time (including adding an element already present, which leaves the set unchanged). The numeric value must be updated whenever the set changes so that it always equals the number of distinct elements currently in the set.

Model the control state and data state abstractly: the data state includes the current set (a finite subset of the universe) and the current stored size (a nonnegative integer). Define initial conditions in which the set is empty and the stored size is zero. Define transitions that represent selecting an element from the universe and adding it to the set, together with the corresponding update to the stored size.

Specify correctness properties: (1) safety — invariance that the stored size equals the true cardinality of the set at all reachable states; (2) type and bound invariants — the set remains a subset of the universe and the stored size is within valid numeric bounds (nonnegative and no larger than the universe size); and (3) liveness — every element of the universe can eventually be added (if desired), so the model permits execution sequences that reach any desired subset. Do not constrain the implementation technique for computing cardinality; allow abstract or recursive definitions as needed but require that they satisfy the invariants.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a very small state machine for a circulating token represented as a record with fields pos, q, and color. The token is constrained by a type invariant: pos ranges over the node identifiers 0..N-1 where N = 3, q is an integer, and color is either "white" or "black". The initial state fixes the token to pos 0, q 0, and color black, and the only next-state action is stuttering via UNCHANGED token, so the system never changes state after initialization.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module RecMem1627 is a minimal stub or skeleton specification modeling a token-passing system, likely intended as a starting point or record/memory fixture for a larger algorithm (such as a termination detection protocol based on a circulating token).

The single variable `token` is a record with three fields: `pos`, an integer representing the token's current position among `N` (three) nodes numbered 0 through 2; `q`, an integer counter; and `color`, drawn from the set `{"white", "black"}`. The `TypeOK` invariant asserts that `token` always belongs to the type `Token`, defined as the set of all such records. The initial state sets the token at position 0, with counter 0 and color "black". The next-state relation is `UNCHANGED token`, meaning no transitions ever modify the token; the system is entirely static after initialization. There is no temporal property, fairness condition, or liveness specification defined. In its current form, the module is effectively a placeholder or test fixture that initializes a token record and then remains frozen, serving to define the data types and initial conditions without specifying any actual system behavior.
desc_intent:
Model a distributed token-circulation protocol on a unidirectional ring of a fixed number N > 1 of processes. The ring has exactly one logical token that moves between neighboring processes. The token carries a small integer counter and a color bit from the set {white, black}. The system must support asynchronous moves of the token: at any step, the token may be handed from its current holder to its clockwise neighbor, optionally updating the counter or flipping the color according to allowed local rules. Specify the legal state space, the initial condition (token owned by process 0, counter zero, color black), and the allowed state transitions for the token movement and local updates.

Require and formalize the following correctness properties:
- Safety: At all times exactly one token exists and the token’s position is always a valid ring process identifier.
- Invariant bounds: The counter remains within a specified integer range (for example, nonnegative and bounded above by a constant).
- Liveness: From any reachable state, the token will eventually visit every process infinitely often (strong fairness or eventual circulation).
- Color consistency: If the color is used to detect a global condition (e.g., termination detection), express the intended relationship between colors and counter values that must hold when the token returns to a designated coordinator process.
- Absence of deadlock: No reachable nonterminal state should have no outgoing transition.

Do not prescribe implementation details such as data structures or atomic steps; describe only the abstract token, processes, initial configuration, transition relation, and the above correctness properties to be checked.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a simple state machine over a set of records and a Boolean flag. The system starts with ok = TRUE and an empty set of records, then in each step recomputes ok' from the current records and either inserts a fixed record, increments the age field of an existing record via a record EXCEPT update, or stutters on recs. The invariant asserts that every record currently in recs has age < 15, and the next-state relation is written to maintain and observe that age-related condition.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module `RecordExcept987` is a small test or model-checking utility that exercises TLA+ record construction and the `EXCEPT` update syntax with a typed record structure.

The specification maintains two variables: `recs`, a set of records each carrying six fields (`id`, `name`, `oneMoreField`, `age`, `isShadow`, and `isAllow`), and `ok`, a Boolean. In the initial state, `ok` is `TRUE` and `recs` is empty. On each step, `ok'` is updated to reflect whether every record in the current `recs` has an age strictly less than 15. The next-state relation then nondeterministically chooses one of three actions: adding a fixed new record named `"foo"` with age 10 and specific field values; replacing an existing record `r` with a copy whose `age` field is incremented by one (only if the incremented record actually differs from the original); or leaving `recs` unchanged. The invariant `Inv` asserts that every record in `recs` has an age less than 15. Because the age-increment action can raise a record's age to 15 or beyond, and the add action introduces a record with age 10 that can subsequently be incremented, the invariant is eventually violated, making this a functional test of record `EXCEPT` expressions and multi-field record typing rather than a model of a real system.
desc_intent:
Specify a system that manages a set of records representing entities with several immutable identity fields and several mutable attributes (including an integer age and some boolean flags). The system must allow adding a new record with fixed values for all fields, and it must allow incrementing the age of an existing record, producing a new record that replaces the old one. Adding the same record twice should not create duplicates: the set of records must behave as a mathematical set (no duplicates). When updating age, the update must actually change the record (the new record must not be syntactically identical to the old one). The system should also permit steps that leave the set unchanged.

Model the system as an unbounded discrete-state transition system over a set of records. Require that initially the set is empty and the system starts in a valid state. The primary safety invariant is that every record’s age remains strictly less than a fixed upper bound (15) at all times. The specification must assert that every transition preserves this invariant. Also specify that the “add” transition always produces a well-formed record with all fields defined, and the “increment age” transition only applies to an existing record and yields a record whose age is one greater. Finally, include a liveness property that from any reachable state it is always possible to either add a new record, increment some record’s age (without violating the age bound), or stutter (do nothing).

desc_declarative_gpt: This module models a simple set-growing system together with a recursively defined cardinality function over finite subsets of integers. The key design idea is to encode recursion without a top-level RECURSIVE definition, by using a bounded CHOOSE over functions from SUBSET S to Int and constraining that function to satisfy the recursive cardinality equations. The specification initializes an empty integer set with size 0, then repeatedly adds a fresh integer from 1..10 while incrementing the tracked size, and states an invariant asserting that the tracked size equals the recursively defined cardinality of the current set.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module demonstrates defining recursive functions in TLA+ without using explicit recursive definition syntax, following the pattern from *Specifying Systems* (p. 67). It models a growing set of integers and tracks its cardinality.

The `Card` operator computes the cardinality of a set `S` by selecting, via a bounded `CHOOSE`, a function `f` over all subsets of `S` mapping to integers, such that `f` satisfies the recursive cardinality relation: the empty set maps to 0, and every non-empty subset `T` maps to one more than the cardinality of `T` with one element removed. The result is `f[S]`.

The state consists of two variables: `Set`, a set of integers, and `size`, an integer counter. Initially both are empty/zero. Each step nondeterministically picks an integer `x` from 1 to 10 that is not already in `Set`, adds it to `Set`, and increments `size` by one. The invariant `Inv` asserts that `Card(Set)` always equals `size`, verifying that the recursively defined cardinality function agrees with the explicitly maintained counter throughout all reachable states. The module also notes that the approach requires expanding the function set `[SUBSET S -> Int]`, which was unsupported in Apalache v0.6.0.
desc_intent:
Specify a system that models a procedure for incrementally constructing a finite set of integers drawn from a bounded universe, while maintaining a separately stored integer that represents the set’s cardinality. The model should allow nondeterministic addition of distinct elements until the set may contain any subset of the allowed universe, and it should maintain the invariant that the stored integer exactly equals the number of elements currently in the set.

Define the abstract state as the current set and the numeric counter, and allow an operation that nondeterministically selects a value from a fixed finite range and adds it to the set only if it is not already present, incrementing the counter accordingly. The initial state should be the empty set with counter zero. The model must permit repeated additions until the set reaches arbitrary subsets of the universe, but must never allow removals or counter manipulation that diverges from actual size changes.

Specify and prove the following correctness properties:
- Safety: the stored counter always equals the cardinality of the set.
- Progress/liveness: from any reachable state that is not the full set, it is possible to add another element (i.e., there is an enabled add operation), ensuring the system can grow toward any larger subset.
- Boundedness: the counter stays within 0 and the size of the fixed universe, and the set remains a subset of that universe.

Do not prescribe a specific syntactic method for computing cardinality; instead state the required relation between the set and the counter and allow any implementation that preserves it.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a small TLA+ test specification about using the Repeat operator with a locally defined operator inside a LET expression. It defines a local operator Op(a, i) == a + 1 and then existentially quantifies over x in the singleton set {5} to assert that Repeat(Op, x, 0) = 5. The spec also includes trivial Init and Next definitions equal to TRUE, and it does not contain temporal properties, fairness conditions, proofs, or PlusCal code.
desc_intent:
Specify a system that models a higher-order repetition operator which applies a given unary operation repeatedly a fixed number of times. The model should treat the operation as an abstract function from integers to integers and the repetition count as a nonnegative integer literal constant. The system must accept any integer-returning operation and any concrete, finite repetition count, and it must compute the result of composing the operation with itself that many times, starting from a given integer initial value.

The specification must allow reasoning about the correctness of the repeated application: for any chosen operation f, any nonnegative integer n (a literal constant), and any initial value v, the repeated application should produce f^n(v) (the n-fold composition of f applied to v). It must ensure that when n = 0 the result equals the initial value, and when n > 0 the result equals f applied to the result of repeating f n-1 times. The model must admit concrete examples to validate this behavior and support proving that for a particular operation and literal count, the computed result equals an expected integer value. Specify invariants and properties that capture these identities and that rule out misinterpretations where the repetition count is not enforced as a literal constant.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module defines a collection of invariant-style checks over the operator Repeat imported from the Apalache module. It tests Repeat with several kinds of operators: a constant increment operator, an accumulating operator that adds the iteration index, a cyclical operator modulo 3, an idempotent set-flattening operator using UNION, and a nilpotent operator that repeatedly removes maximal elements from a set. The specification itself is trivial at the temporal level with Init == TRUE and Next == TRUE, while the main asserted content is the conjunction Inv of the five properties describing expected behavior of Repeat under these different algebraic patterns.
desc_intent:
Specify a generic operator-iteration facility and prove key algebraic invariants about repeated application of a binary-indexed unary operator. Model a system that takes as parameters (1) a deterministic state value from an arbitrary domain, (2) a natural number count n, and (3) a family of unary transformations indexed by iteration number (each transformation may depend on the current index). The facility should compute the result of applying, in sequence, the operator at index 0, then index 1, … up to index n-1, starting from the initial state, returning the final state after n steps.

Require the model to support abstract instantiations of the operator so that the same iteration mechanism can be used to reason about multiple algebraic behaviors. For a number of illustrative operator instances, state and verify these correctness properties about the iterated result:
- Additive accumulation: iterate an operator that adds a fixed constant and show the result equals the initial state plus n times that constant.
- Summation-of-indices: iterate an operator that adds the current index and show the result equals the initial state plus the sum 0..(n-1).
- Periodicity: for an operator whose k-fold composition equals the identity, show the result after any multiple of k steps equals the initial state.
- Idempotence: for an operator whose composition twice equals itself, show that applying it once and then any further number of times yields the same result as applying it once.
- Nilpotence: for an operator that becomes the constant zero-state after some finite number of iterations, show that once the zero-state is reached it remains zero on further iterations.

Do not commit to a particular implementation strategy; the model should be abstract, parametric over the operator and the domain, and include assertions or invariants that capture the algebraic properties above for verification.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module models safe arithmetic operations over 256-bit unsigned integers in the style of Solidity's SafeMath library. It defines helper operators for checked addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulo, and then nondeterministically tests selected operations by choosing in-range integer arguments and storing the result together with an error flag. The specification is expected to deadlock after one test step, and it checks arithmetic correctness conditions as invariants relating the stored result and error flag to the mathematically exact integer result.
desc_declarative_claude:
This module is a test specification for verifying the correctness of SafeMath arithmetic operations modeled after OpenZeppelin's Solidity SafeMath library, which provides overflow-safe integer arithmetic for 256-bit unsigned integers.

The module defines five variables: `opcode` (the current operation being tested), `arg1` and `arg2` (the two operands), `res` (the result), and `is_error` (a flag indicating whether the operation detected an overflow or invalid condition). The system starts in a `NOP` state with all values zeroed. In a single `Next` step, the system non-deterministically selects two 256-bit unsigned integers and applies either `TryAdd` or `TrySub` (multiplication, division, and modulo are commented out as too expensive for Z3), then transitions to a terminal stuttering state where variables remain unchanged. The `TryAdd` and `TrySub` functions mimic SafeMath's overflow detection logic: addition fails when the modular result wraps below either operand, and subtraction fails when the subtrahend exceeds the minuend.

The invariants `InvAdd`, `InvSub`, `InvMul`, `InvDiv`, and `InvMod` assert that `is_error` is set exactly when the mathematically precise integer result would overflow or involve division by zero. The spec is explicitly expected to deadlock (after one operation step) without violating any invariant. A separate `FalseInv` property, intended to be falsified, asserts that the sum of the two arguments never reaches `MAX_UNSIGNED`, serving as a demonstration that overflows can be witnessed.
desc_intent:
Specify a model of an unsigned fixed-width arithmetic checker that nondeterministically tests basic arithmetic operations on two nonnegative integers interpreted modulo 2^N (for a configurable bit width N). The system should repeatedly choose an operation code from {ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV, MOD} and two operands in the valid unsigned range [0, 2^N − 1], and produce a pair: a boolean flag indicating whether the operation failed (due to overflow or invalid arguments) and an unsigned result value (the machine result modulo 2^N when defined). The model must reflect the semantics expected from defensive arithmetic routines that detect overflow/divide-by-zero instead of wrapping silently:
- Addition should report failure if the true integer sum exceeds 2^N − 1; otherwise it must return the exact sum.
- Subtraction should report failure if the true integer difference is negative; otherwise it must return the exact difference.
- Multiplication should report failure if the true integer product exceeds 2^N − 1; otherwise it must return the exact product.
- Division and modulo should report failure on division by zero; otherwise they must return the mathematical quotient or remainder.

State that operands are always within the unsigned range before the operation, and that results when not failing equal the mathematical result (not a wrapped value) and are in range. Specify safety properties to verify:
- The checker never returns a success flag with a result that disagrees with the true mathematical result.
- The checker flags every case where the mathematical result would be out of range or undefined (e.g., divide/mod by zero).
Also request an invariant to detect deadlock-free progress of the testing loop (i.e., the system should always be able to pick the next test) and ask to parameterize the bit width N so proofs can be attempted for typical widths (e.g., 256).

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a simple sequence-filtering computation over a single variable `myseq`. It defines a recursive helper inside `Select` that scans a sequence from the head and returns the suffix beginning at the first element satisfying a supplied test predicate; if no element satisfies the predicate, it returns the empty sequence. The behavior initializes `myseq` to `<< 1, 2, 3 >>` and then updates it in one step to the result of applying `Select` with a locally defined evenness test, so the next state keeps only the suffix starting from the first even element.
desc_declarative_claude: The module defines a simple single-step state machine that demonstrates a higher-order `Select` operator on sequences. The sole variable `myseq` is initialized to the sequence ⟨1, 2, 3⟩. The `Select` operator takes a sequence and a unary predicate and recursively filters the sequence, returning the first element for which the predicate holds — effectively finding the first matching element rather than collecting all matches, because once a matching head is found it is returned directly without continuing recursion. The `Next` action defines `IsEven` as a local predicate and sets `myseq'` to the result of calling `Select` on the current `myseq` with `IsEven`, which will yield ⟨2⟩ (the subsequence starting from the first even element). No temporal specification, fairness conditions, invariants, or properties are declared; the module is essentially a test or demonstration wrapper that exercises the recursive higher-order `Select` function rather than modeling a real concurrent system.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal model of a pure selection operation on finite sequences: given an initial finite sequence of integers and a predicate on integers, the system should produce as its next state the first element of the sequence that satisfies the predicate, or an empty sequence/value that denotes “no selection” if no element satisfies the predicate. The model should treat the predicate as an abstract, boolean test that can be evaluated on any element, and the initial sequence should be a fixed finite sequence of known integers.

The specification must capture the state transition that replaces the current sequence by the selection result computed from the current sequence and the predicate. It must allow repeated application of this transition (so the selected result can be observed as a state). The model must guarantee that:
- If an element satisfying the predicate exists in the sequence, the new state equals that element (i.e., the selection returns the first such element).
- If no element satisfies the predicate, the new state represents “no element selected” (e.g., an empty sequence or distinct sentinel).
- The selection preserves order: the element returned is the earliest in the original sequence satisfying the predicate.
- No other changes to the state occur besides replacing the sequence with the selection result.

Also specify simple liveness/termination expectations: the selection transition is always enabled and deterministically yields the described result in one step. Include invariants expressing the deterministic nature and the correspondence between the prestate sequence and the poststate selection.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a small test specification for the Sequences operator SelectSeq. It defines a fixed integer sequence and several predicate operators, then asserts invariants characterizing how SelectSeq filters the sequence under predicates that always pass, always fail, select even elements, or select elements greater than 1. The module also includes a minimal state with one variable and simple Init and Next definitions, but it does not define a temporal Spec or any fairness or proof structure.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal model of a deterministic sequence-filtering operator that takes a finite sequence of integers and a predicate over integers and returns the subsequence of elements that satisfy the predicate, preserving their original order. The model should treat the sequence and predicate as inputs and allow arbitrary finite sequences (including empty) and arbitrary decidable predicates on integers.

Require that the operator:
- Returns a sequence that contains only elements from the input sequence that satisfy the predicate.
- Preserves the relative order of selected elements as in the input.
- Produces an empty sequence when no input elements satisfy the predicate.
- Produces the original sequence when every element satisfies the predicate.
- Is deterministic: the same input sequence and predicate always produce the same output.

Specify additional sanity properties to check:
- Length monotonicity: the output length is at most the input length.
- Element correspondence: every element of the output appears at some index in the input and satisfies the predicate; conversely, every input element that satisfies the predicate appears in the output.
- Idempotence: applying the operator twice with the same predicate yields the same result as applying it once.

Model initial states and transitions only as needed to exercise and verify these properties; avoid committing to a particular implementation strategy.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a simple transition system over three integer-like state variables x, y, and z. The initial state fixes x = 0, y = 1, and z = 2, and the Next action constrains the primed values of the variables using nested conjunctions and disjunctions of membership tests over singleton sets. The module does not include an explicit temporal specification such as Spec, no fairness conditions, no fault model, and no stated safety or liveness theorem; it is essentially a small action-level example illustrating selections among possible next-state assignments.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies a simple transition system over three integer variables `x`, `y`, and `z`. It serves primarily as a model-checking test or utility example demonstrating how TLA+ handles conjunctive and disjunctive primed-variable assignments within a `Next` action.

The initial state sets `x = 0`, `y = 1`, and `z = 2`. The `Next` relation is a conjunction of four top-level conjuncts, each constraining the next values of the variables through nested disjunctions. The first conjunct requires `y'` to be either 1 or 2, and independently requires `x'` to be 3, 4, or (simultaneously) `z' = 5` and `y' = 6`. The second conjunct requires `z'` to be either 7 or 8. The third conjunct requires `x'` to be either 9 or (simultaneously) both 10 and 11 — the latter being unsatisfiable since `x'` cannot equal both 10 and 11 at once. Because all four top-level conjuncts must hold simultaneously and variables like `x'`, `y'`, and `z'` are constrained by multiple conjuncts with conflicting requirements, the overall `Next` relation is effectively unsatisfiable, meaning no transition from any state is possible. There is no temporal specification, fairness condition, or named invariant or property defined in the module.
desc_intent:
Specify a small-state transition system that models a component making nondeterministic selections from a set of discrete choices over time. The model should start in a fixed initial state where three finite-valued state elements have particular initial values. At each step the component may update one or more of these elements by choosing values from specified finite sets; some choices are independent while others are constrained to occur together (i.e., certain combinations of simultaneous assignments are allowed or disallowed). Model the selection behavior as nondeterministic: any allowed choice may be taken at a step so long as it respects the combination constraints.

Require that the model capture reachable-state exploration under fair nondeterminism (no starvation of enabled choices). Specify invariants expressing that every state variable always takes a value from its intended finite domain. Specify safety properties forbidding certain forbidden combinations of values (for example, never allow two particular values to hold simultaneously, and never allow an illegal simultaneous assignment pattern). Specify basic liveness goals: from any reachable state it must always be possible to eventually reach a state in which a designated variable assumes each of its allowed values (i.e., each choice is eventually taken). Also require that if a transition chooses to change one variable in a way that requires another variable to take a particular dependent value, that dependent value must hold immediately in the same step. The specification should be abstract (no implementation details) and suitable for model checking.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a simple parametric set-update system with one state variable, `set`, and a constant set `Values`. The system starts with `set = {}` and each step either adds one element from `Values \\ set` to the set or removes one element currently in the set. The comments explain that the model is used as a regression test for set union behavior and checks an invariant stating that the set is not equal to the full set of values, even though the comments note that the full set is reachable in exactly N steps.
desc_intent:
Model a finite-state system that maintains a subset drawn from a fixed finite universe of values. The system begins with the empty subset and evolves in discrete steps. At each step, it may either add a single value not currently present or remove a single value that is currently present. The model should be parametric in the size and contents of the universe so different finite sets of values can be plugged in.

Specify safety and liveness requirements. Safety: any state reached must always be a subset of the universe (no spurious elements). Also specify an invariant expressing that a particular “bad” configuration — the subset equal to the entire universe — is considered undesirable. The model should enable checking whether that bad configuration is reachable from the initial empty set.

Liveness: if additions are repeatedly chosen, the system should be able to reach the full-universe configuration in exactly as many additive steps as the universe has elements; conversely, provide the ability to remove elements so the system need not remain full once achieved. Ensure nondeterministic choice between add and remove actions is represented so multiple interleavings and schedules can be explored. Include a property that counts or bounds the minimum number of steps required to reach the full set.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a simple lossy message transmission system with three set-valued state variables: a sender set, a receiver set, and a transmission medium set. Initially, all values are in the sender, while the receiver and medium are empty; messages may be sent from sender to medium, dropped from the medium, or received into the receiver without being removed from the medium. The intended regression-test scenario checks behavior of set difference in the presence of existentially chosen elements, and the invariant asserts that not all three components are empty at the same time.
desc_declarative_claude:
This module is a regression test for the Apalache model checker, specifically targeting correct handling of oracles in set-minus operations. It models a simple lossy message-transmission system with three components: a sender, a transmission medium, and a receiver, each represented as a set of integer values.

The single constant `Values` is initialized (via `CInit`) to the integer range `0..6`, and the three variables `sender`, `receiver`, and `medium` are all sets of integers. Initially, `sender` holds all values in `Values`, while `receiver` and `medium` are empty.

Three actions define the next-state relation. `Snd` non-deterministically picks a message from `sender`, removes it, and places it into `medium`. `Drop` non-deterministically removes a message from `medium` without delivering it, modeling lossy transmission. `Rcv` non-deterministically picks a message from `medium` and adds it to `receiver` without removing it from `medium`, reflecting that multiple copies may be in transit and making the state space larger. The overall `Next` relation is the disjunction of these three actions.

The invariant `Inv` asserts that at least one of the three sets is non-empty. Because messages can be dropped and the medium is not cleared on receive, it is possible for all of `sender`, `medium`, and `receiver` to become empty simultaneously, meaning the invariant is reachable in violation within `2*N` steps for `N` messages. The module carries no fairness conditions or liveness properties.
desc_intent:
Specify a model of a simple lossy message-delivery system with three components: a sender that initially holds a finite set of messages to transmit, a transmission medium that can carry zero or more messages (and may drop some), and a receiver that accumulates messages it observes. The system should allow the following behaviors: the sender may pick a message it still holds and place a copy into the medium (removing it from the sender’s local set); the medium may nondeterministically drop any message it currently carries; and the receiver may nondeterministically observe (receive) any message present in the medium, adding it to its local set without removing the message from the medium (i.e., reception does not consume the medium’s copy). The model should assume a finite, nonempty universe of possible message values.

Specify as correctness requirements that (1) the system never reaches a state in which all three components are simultaneously empty (i.e., at least one of sender, medium, or receiver always contains some message), and (2) the model explores the possibility that not all messages must be lost — there should exist executions where at least one original message is eventually present at the receiver. Also require that the model supports nondeterminism in action ordering and allows multiple copies of the same value in transit conceptually through the medium’s set semantics. Finally, state liveness and safety properties to check: safety — the triple-empty state is unreachable; liveness — there exists an execution in which the receiver eventually contains some message originally held by the sender.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification defines a very small TLA+ module that introduces a higher-order operator L, which applies an operator argument F to an input n. The system behavior itself is trivial: both Init and Next are defined as TRUE, so the state space is unconstrained and no meaningful transition structure or fault model is modeled. The main property expressed in the file is Inv, which checks that applying L to the identity lambda and the value 3 yields 3, demonstrating use of a LAMBDA expression and operator application.
desc_intent:
Specify a simple functional-evaluation system that models first-class anonymous functions (lambdas) and their application to arguments. The model should represent lambda expressions as values that can be created, passed around, and invoked; it should allow nested or higher-order lambdas (lambdas that return or accept other lambdas). The system must include an evaluation mechanism that applies a lambda to an argument and yields the correct result according to lexical scoping and parameter substitution semantics.

Requirements:
- Creation: The model must support creating an anonymous function that binds a parameter and has a body expression.
- Application: There must be a well-defined operation that applies a function value to an argument value and returns the result of evaluating the body with the parameter bound to the argument.
- Determinism: Application must be deterministic: given the same function value and argument, the evaluation produces the same result.
- Type/arity safety: The model must ensure functions are applied with the correct number of arguments; ill-formed applications should be disallowed or produce a defined error value.
- Simple correctness property: For a lambda that returns its parameter unchanged, applying it to a concrete value must yield that value.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a very small symbolic transition system with a single state variable named state. desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies the **Klotski sliding-block puzzle**, a classic combinatorial puzzle played on a 4×5 grid. The single variable `board` represents the current state of the puzzle as a set of pieces, where each piece is a set of grid positions (pairs of integers) that it occupies.

The board is initialized to the standard Klotski configuration (`Klotski`), which places ten pieces of varying sizes on a 4×5 grid, leaving two cells empty. The `Next` relation computes the set of currently unoccupied positions and, for each empty cell, considers the four cardinal neighbors that are occupied by some piece. A piece adjacent to an empty cell can slide into that empty space provided its entire translated footprint lies within the grid bounds and does not overlap any other piece. The `update` operator computes all boards reachable by such a single slide, and `Next` nondeterministically chooses one of them.

The invariant `TypeOK` asserts that `board` is always a set of pieces (subsets of grid positions). The reachability goal `KlotskiGoal` checks whether the 2×2 block occupying positions `{<<1,3>>, <<1,4>>, <<2,3>>, <<2,4>>}` is present in `board`, representing the puzzle's winning condition — sliding the large square piece to the bottom-center exit. The module is a typed variant (annotated with Apalache type comments) of the original TLA+ Examples `SlidingPuzzles` specification.
desc_intent:

Two temporal properties over actions are defined. `Liveness` asserts that eventually the action `x' = x + 1` occurs as a stuttering-sensitive action (i.e., `<<x' = x + 1>>_x`, a non-stuttering step where `x` increases by one), which holds along the counter's normal progression before the reset. `FalseLiveness` asserts that eventually it is always the case that `[x' = x + 1]_x` holds — meaning from some point forward every step either increments `x` by one or is a stuttering step — which is false because the counter periodically resets from 3 to 0, violating the condition infinitely often. The module appears designed to illustrate and check temporal properties expressed directly over action formulas, distinguishing between a property that is satisfiable along the trace and one that fails due to the reset behavior.
desc_intent:

The module defines two variables over a fixed process set `Procs = 1..4`: `unchecked`, a function mapping each process to a set of integers, and `nxt`, a function mapping each process to a single integer. Initially, every process has an empty `unchecked` set and `nxt` value of 1.

The `Next` relation allows one of two things to happen: either some process `self` nondeterministically picks an element `i` from its `unchecked` set and updates `nxt[self]` to that value, with the additional guard that the newly assigned `nxt'[self]` must still belong to `unchecked[self]`, leaving `unchecked` unchanged; or the system stutters with no state change. The notable feature being tested is the use of a primed variable (`nxt'`) in a guard condition within the same action that assigns it, which is the pattern that triggered the Apalache issue. No invariants, liveness properties, or temporal specification are defined.
desc_intent:

The model must allow the candidate sets to be read (to choose a new pointer value) but not modified by the step that updates the pointer; non-deterministic choices must be explicitly modeled so a process can only assign its pointer to a value that currently belongs to its own candidate set.

Also require that pointer updates do not affect candidate sets or other processes’ pointers. Include any stuttering step that leaves the entire state unchanged. desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a trivial system with no constants, variables, or state structure. desc_intent:

The specification should capture the notion that the system itself imposes no constraint on state evolution, while an external correctness requirement asserts a property that must hold at every reachable state but deliberately cannot hold.

Describe the state space broadly (it may be unconstrained or contain any values), allow a transition relation that always enables a next step from every state, and assert an invariant predicate that evaluates to false for all states. The model must include checks that exercise both safety and liveness reasoning: show that the invariant is required to hold at all times (safety requirement) and that the system nevertheless allows infinite progress (liveness requirement). desc_declarative_gpt: This module defines typed inductive invariants for a two-phase commit specification imported from the extended module `TwoPhaseTyped`. desc_intent:
Specify a formal model of the two‑phase commit protocol between a single transaction manager and a fixed set of resource managers. The model should describe the states each participant can occupy (including initial, working/prepared, committed, and aborted), the messages that can be sent (e.g., prepare, prepared, commit, abort), and the allowed ways the protocol may progress while permitting asynchronous, unreliable delivery but not message duplication beyond what the underlying message set models.

Requirements:
- The transaction manager may initiate a prepare phase and then decide to commit or abort; resource managers independently respond to prepare by moving to prepared or aborting.
- If any resource manager reaches committed, then the transaction manager must be committed.
- If the transaction manager is committed, every resource manager must have been prepared and no resource manager may be in working or aborted; a commit message must be present.
- If the transaction manager is aborted, an abort message must be present.
- For each resource manager: if it is recorded as prepared, it cannot be in working; if it is working then no prepared message exists; a prepared message implies the resource manager is not working; if it is aborted then either an abort message exists or there is no prepared message for it.
- Any abort message must be justified: it must come from the transaction manager being aborted or from some resource manager that aborted without having been recorded prepared.
- Any commit message must imply that all resource managers were recorded prepared, and the commit is associated either with the transaction manager being committed or with at least one resource manager being committed.

Guarantee invariants capturing type/safety (well‑formed sets/states), a consistency relation between transaction manager and resource manager views, and the above safety properties that rule out contradictory states (e.g., a committed resource when transaction manager not committed). Do not prescribe a particular implementation; model possible asynchronous interleavings that respect these invariants.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a small type-definition companion module for a typed two-phase commit specification. desc_intent:
Specify a formal TLA+ model of a two-phase commit protocol between a single coordinator and multiple participants (resource managers). The system must capture asynchronous message passing of three message kinds: prepare notifications, commit decisions, and abort decisions. Model participant behavior that can vote to prepare or fail to prepare, and the coordinator behavior that decides commit only when all participants have prepared; otherwise it must decide abort. Include possible message loss, duplication, and reordering, but assume eventual delivery if retried (or model unreliable channels with explicit resend actions). Allow participants and the coordinator to crash and later recover, retaining durable logs for their locally persisted decisions and votes.

Specify safety properties: agreement (no two non-failed processes decide differently), validity (a commit decision occurs only if every participant had previously prepared), and atomicity (either all non-faulty participants ultimately commit or all abort). Specify liveness properties under suitable assumptions (e.g., eventual reliable communication and bounded crashes): eventual termination (every non-faulty participant eventually decides) and coordinator progress (if all participants prepare and no further failures occur, the system eventually commits). Also require that durable logging ensures decisions survive crashes and that recovery respects logged state. Provide the abstract state space, message semantics, and the invariants to verify these properties.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a typed version of the classic two-phase commit protocol. It models a transaction manager and a set of resource managers, with state variables for each RM's local state, the TM state, the set of prepared RMs known to the TM, and the set of messages that have been sent. The specification defines initialization, the TM and RM actions, a next-state relation, the overall temporal specification TPSpec, and a consistency property TCConsistent stating that no two resource managers can end in conflicting committed and aborted decisions.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies the Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol, adapted from Leslie Lamport's canonical TLA+ example and annotated with Apalache type annotations. It models a transaction manager (TM) coordinating a set of resource managers (RMs) to reach a consistent commit or abort decision.

The constant `RM` is the set of resource managers. The variables are `rmState`, a function mapping each RM to one of `"working"`, `"prepared"`, `"committed"`, or `"aborted"`; `tmState`, the TM's state (`"init"`, `"committed"`, or `"aborted"`); `tmPrepared`, the set of RMs from which the TM has received Prepared messages; and `msgs`, the set of messages in transit, drawn from typed variants `Commit`, `Abort`, and `Prepared(rm)`. Initially, all RMs are working, the TM is in `"init"`, and no messages have been sent.

The TM actions are: `TMRcvPrepared`, which records receipt of a Prepared message from an RM; `TMCommit`, which transitions the TM to committed and broadcasts a Commit message once all RMs have prepared; and `TMAbort`, which spontaneously moves the TM to aborted and broadcasts an Abort message. The RM actions are: `RMPrepare`, which moves an RM from working to prepared and sends a Prepared message; `RMChooseToAbort`, which moves an RM directly to aborted; `RMRcvCommitMsg`, which commits an RM upon seeing the Commit message; and `RMRcvAbortMsg`, which aborts an RM upon seeing the Abort message. The temporal specification `TPSpec` is a safety-only stuttering-closed formula with no fairness. The invariant `TCConsistent` asserts that no two RMs ever reach conflicting decisions.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal TLA+ model of the classic two‑phase commit protocol (one transaction manager coordinating a fixed set of resource managers). The model should describe the protocol at the message/event level (prepare, prepared, commit, abort) and capture the possible asynchronous interactions and independent failures/choices of participants. The system must allow resource managers to: initially be in a working state, choose to prepare (sending a prepared indication), or unilaterally decide to abort; the transaction manager must start in an initial state, collect prepared indications from resource managers, and either decide to commit when every resource manager has prepared or spontaneously decide to abort; once the TM decides, it must broadcast the corresponding global decision (commit or abort) that resource managers can later receive. Messages can be delayed and delivered in any order; no message loss is assumed.

Require the following key safety properties:
- Consistency: no two resource managers may end up with conflicting final decisions (one committed while another aborted).
- Agreement with global decision: if the transaction manager decides commit (resp. abort), then eventually every resource manager that has not aborted will reach the committed (resp. aborted) final state.
- Validity: a resource manager may commit only if either (a) it prepared and the TM later decided commit, or (b) it received the TM’s commit; it must not commit without those prerequisites.

Also require a type/structure invariant that bounds states and messages, and formulate an initial condition where all RMs are working, the TM is initial, and no messages exist. Include liveness/temporal goals optionally (e.g., eventual delivery of TM’s decision to non‑failed RMs) but ensure safety properties above are mandatory.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a two-phase commit protocol in an uninterpreted first-order logic style derived from Lamport's TwoPhase specification. It models a transaction manager and a set of resource managers, representing resource-manager states, transaction-manager state, and message presence with uninterpreted functions and Boolean predicates rather than richer TLA+ data structures. The specification defines initialization, transaction-manager and resource-manager actions, a next-state relation, a temporal safety-style system specification TPSpec, and a consistency predicate asserting that no two resource managers can end in conflicting committed and aborted states.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module TwoPhaseUFO is a reformulation of Leslie Lamport's classic Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol rewritten in Uninterpreted First-Order Logic (UFOL), a fragment of TLA+. Its purpose is to represent the same protocol using only uninterpreted sorts and predicates rather than concrete set-theoretic constructs, making it amenable to first-order logic reasoning and model checking tools that operate on that fragment.

The constant `Values_RM` represents the set of resource managers (of sort `SORT_RM`). The variables track each RM's state (`rmState`, a function from RMs to an uninterpreted state sort), the transaction manager's state (`tmState`), the set of RMs from which the TM has received Prepared messages (`tmPrepared`, a Boolean-valued predicate over RMs), and three message-presence flags: `msgsPrepared` (per-RM Boolean), `msgsCommit` (global Boolean), and `msgsAbort` (global Boolean). State values such as "working," "prepared," "committed," and "aborted" are represented as distinguished uninterpreted constants suffixed with `_OF_SORT_STATE`.

Initially all RMs are working, the TM is in its init state, and all message flags are false. Actions include the TM receiving a Prepared message from a specific RM, the TM committing (once all RMs are prepared), and the TM aborting spontaneously. RM actions allow each RM to prepare, choose to abort unilaterally, receive a Commit message, or receive an Abort message. The temporal specification `TPSpec` is a safety specification (no fairness conditions). The invariant `TCConsistent` asserts that no RM has committed while another has aborted, enforcing the fundamental consistency requirement of atomic commitment.
desc_intent: Specify a formal model of the Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol for a distributed transaction involving a single transaction coordinator (transaction manager) and an arbitrary finite set of resource managers. The model should describe the allowed states and asynchronous message-driven interactions, not an implementation. It must include: initial conditions where every resource manager is in a local "working" state and the coordinator is in an initial state; actions by a resource manager to decide to prepare (move to prepared) or to locally choose to abort (move to aborted) without sending messages; the ability of a resource manager to receive and act upon a global Commit or Abort instruction (transition to committed or aborted respectively); the coordinator receiving prepare notifications from resource managers, collecting them, and when all resource managers have prepared, issuing a Commit; and the coordinator being able to spontaneously decide to Abort. Model messages abstractly as delivery predicates (i.e., whether a Commit, Abort, or a given RM’s Prepared notification has been received), allowing asynchronous delivery and independent ordering. Specify safety properties: (1) consistency — no two resource managers may end up with conflicting final decisions (one committed while another aborted), and (2) validity — if every resource manager prepared and the coordinator issues Commit, then all resource managers that later receive the Commit must move to committed; and (3) that once the coordinator decides Commit (or Abort), it stays in that terminal decision. Also require that state transitions respect the causal flow (e.g., an RM cannot move from working directly to committed unless a Commit is delivered). Do not constrain internal encodings; keep the model at the level of states and message delivery predicates so it can be used to prove these safety invariants under asynchronous message delivery and nondeterministic scheduling.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification is a small regression test for a desugaring issue involving grouped-variable UNCHANGED expressions. desc_intent:

Requirements:

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification is a minimal test module intended to check parsing and typing behavior for UNCHANGED expressions over tuple syntax. desc_intent:

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a single integer-valued state variable x. desc_intent: Specify a formal model of a single integer-valued variable that starts at zero and may evolve over discrete steps according to a deterministic transition rule. desc_intent:

desc_intent: Specify a formal model of a simple verifier that compares two function-valued expressions and determines whether they are equal, even when one or both functions have empty domains. desc_intent:

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a set of processes, each with an integer-valued logical clock and a derived drift value for every ordered pair of processes. desc_declarative_claude:

desc_intent:

desc_intent:

- Deadlock-freedom (progress): if some process tries to enter the critical section, some process will eventually enter the critical section (no system-wide lockout).

desc_declarative_claude:

Each process cycles through labeled steps: ncs (non-critical section), e1–e4 (entry protocol, where the process sets its flag, scans others' numbers to find a maximum, picks a strictly larger ticket, then clears its flag), w1–w2 (waiting loop, spinning until no other process has a smaller lexicographically ordered ⟨num, pid⟩ pair), cs (critical section), and exit (resetting the ticket to zero). desc_declarative_claude:

Each correct process holds a program counter (pc) drawn from {"V0", "V1", "SE", "AC"}, where V0 and V1 represent initial states (not broadcasting or broadcasting), SE means an ECHO message has been sent, and AC means the process has accepted. The shared variable sent tracks all ECHO messages broadcast by correct processes, while rcvd records what each correct process has received, including messages that faulty processes may inject arbitrarily.

In each step, a correct process first nondeterministically receives a subset of sent messages plus any ECHOs from faulty processes, then fires one of four guarded transitions: UponV1 sends an ECHO immediately from state V1; UponNonFaulty sends an ECHO upon receiving between T+1 and N−T−1 ECHOs without yet having sent one; UponAcceptNotSent accepts and sends an ECHO upon receiving N−T or more ECHOs from an initial state; and UponAccept moves to AC from SE upon receiving N−T or more ECHOs. The safety invariant Unforg asserts no correct process reaches AC when all started in V0 (no broadcast initiated). The temporal properties UnforgLtl, CorrLtl, and RelayLtl express unforgeability, eventual acceptance when all started in V1, and relay (if any correct process accepts, eventually all do), respectively.

- Validity: If all correct processes start with value 0, then they should eventually all accept; if all start with value 1, at least one correct process should eventually accept.

desc_intent:

The module specifies a distributed **Maximal Independent Set (MIS)** algorithm running on a graph of `N = 3` nodes, using a three-round message-passing protocol. Each node tracks whether it is `awake`, its current `status` (`"unknown"`, `"winner"`, or `"loser"`), its remaining neighbors `rem_nbrs`, and a per-node inbox `msgs`. The algorithm cycles through three rounds. In **Round 1**, nodes broadcast their current values; a node declares itself a `"winner"` if its value is strictly greater than all received values (unless `HAS_BUG = TRUE`, in which case every awake node unconditionally becomes a winner). In **Round 2**, winners notify their neighbors; a node becomes a `"loser"` if it receives any winner notification. In **Round 3**, losers notify their neighbors, awake status is updated so that only nodes that are neither winners nor losers remain awake, and each node removes its loser neighbors from `rem_nbrs`. The round counter advances modulo 3 on every step.

The `CONSTANT HAS_BUG` toggles a deliberate fault in the winner-election condition. The safety invariant `IsIndependent` asserts that no two adjacent nodes simultaneously hold `"winner"` status. The predicate `Terminated` checks whether all nodes have become inactive, though no explicit liveness property is stated in the module body.

- Capture asynchronous message delivery within a synchronous round: messages sent in a round are delivered to neighbors within that same round before the next round begins.

- Safety: at most one node in any edge may declare itself a winner (no two adjacent winners) — i.e., the set of winners must form an independent set.
- Termination/Progress: eventually every node becomes either a winner or a loser and then sleeps (global termination).
- Consistency: once a node is decided winner (resp. loser), it does not later revert to a different decision.
- Messages are only of three kinds: value proposals, winner announcements, and loser announcements; nodes act only on the content and origin of these messages.
- Allow an optional configuration flag that can enable or disable a modeled bug for testing robustness; when enabled, the model may relax the winner-selection predicate to simulate a faulty comparison.

desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies the **partial link reversal** algorithm on directed graphs, based on the 1981 Gafni–Bertsekas paper on loop-free routing in networks with changing topology. The system models a fixed set of nodes (`Nodes = 1..N`, with `N = 4`) and a designated destination node (`dest = 1`).

The state is captured by three variables: `out`, mapping each node to its set of outgoing neighbors; `in`, the corresponding incoming-neighbor sets (derived as the transpose of `out`); and `to_rev`, tracking which incoming edges each node has already had reversed by prior steps. The initial graph is a fixed directed acyclic graph encoded in `InitOut`, with `in` computed from it and `to_rev` empty everywhere.

At each step, the `Next` action selects a nonempty subset of current **sinks** — nodes with no outgoing edges other than the destination — as the `Active` set. For each active sink, the algorithm computes which incoming edges to reverse via `Reversed`: if not all incoming edges have been previously reversed, only the unreversed ones are flipped; otherwise all incoming edges are reversed. The three update actions then simultaneously rewrite `out`, `in`, and `to_rev` to reflect those reversals. Non-active nodes lose outgoing edges toward active sinks and gain incoming edges from them, while active sinks swap their incoming edges into outgoing ones and reset their `to_rev`.

The module defines `IsDag` as a partial-order embedding condition, intended as a safety invariant asserting that the evolving directed graph remains acyclic throughout execution. No explicit temporal specification or fairness conditions are stated.
desc_intent:
Model a distributed partial link-reversal routing algorithm for a network of nodes forming a directed graph that may be disconnected. The model should represent only abstract nodes and directed edges and must not hard-code local implementation steps.

Requirements:
- Initial state: a directed graph without directed cycles (a DAG), with a distinguished destination node.
- At each step, any nonempty subset of current sinks may act concurrently. Each acting sink may choose a subset of its incoming neighbors whose incident edges it will reverse (turn into outgoing edges for the sink). The rest of the network updates consistently to reflect those reversals.
- After each step the graph must remain acyclic.
- Progress requirement: once a node becomes a sink (other than the destination) it must eventually perform a reversal or cease to be a sink because others reversed edges; overall the system should avoid livelock where some sink forever defers reversal while the network makes no progress toward routing to the destination.
- Safety properties: no node creates self-loops; edge updates are symmetric and consistent (if an edge u->v is removed then v->u is added only when intended).
- Liveness/invariant to guarantee termination under fair scheduling: either each non-destination node eventually has a directed path to the destination, or the set of sinks stabilizes only when no sink exists.

Specify these behaviors and correctness properties abstractly so formal verification can check acyclicity invariants, edge consistency, and the required liveness/progress conditions.

The initial state sets all votes to `init` and places the initial configuration command at instance −1 in `learned`. Three actions drive the system: `VoteFor` lets an acceptor cast a vote in a given instance and ballot, subject to consistency with other votes in that ballot, safety conditions (`SafeAt`), and configuration validity (`ConfigOKAt`); `Abstain` lets an acceptor mark a set of instance-ballot pairs as abstained; and `Learn` adds a command to `learned` when it has been chosen (via a quorum of matching votes) under a valid configuration. The next-state relation `Next` is the disjunction of all such steps, and the temporal specification `Spec` is the standard safety-only formula `Init /\ [][Next]_<<avote, learned>>` with no fairness conditions.

The module states and partially proves two theorems: that `TypeOK` is an invariant, and that the key safety property `SafetyInv`—asserting that at most one command is ever learned per instance—is an invariant. The proof proceeds through an inductive invariant `Inv` with five conjuncts, covering type correctness, ballot-level vote uniqueness, justification of learned entries, well-formedness of the configuration sequence (`CfgOK`), and a detailed `SafeAt`/`ConfigOKAt` witness property for every vote. desc_declarative_gpt: This TLA+ specification models Dijkstra's distributed termination detection algorithm on a ring network, as described in EWD 840. desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies Dijkstra's distributed termination detection algorithm on a ring (EWD 840). The four variables are `active` (a Boolean map over nodes), `color` (a color map over nodes), `tpos` (the current token position), and `tcolor` (the token's color). The `System` actions implement the detection protocol: node 0 initiates a new probe when it holds the token and either it or the token is black, resetting the token to white and itself to white; any other node holding the token passes it to its predecessor, possibly staining the token black if the node itself is black, then whitening itself. These system actions are subject to weak fairness. The `Environment` actions model the underlying computation: an active node may send a message to any other node (activating it and potentially turning the sender black if the message travels against the token direction), or any active node may spontaneously deactivate. Together these actions define a temporal specification `Spec` asserting the initial condition, the always-enabled next-state relation as a safety constraint, and weak fairness of the token-passing actions. The module defines `TypeOK` as a type invariant but does not explicitly state liveness or correctness properties within this file.
desc_intent:

The model should represent processes that can be active or passive, each holding a local color (white or black), and a single circulating token carrying a color. Processes may send activation messages to other processes (possibly wrapping around the ring), which may cause the sender to become black if it activates a process “ahead” in ring order; active processes may become passive at any time. The token moves around the ring in the opposite direction of message activation and can be recolored to black when it passes a black process; a designated initiator can start a probe round by passing a white token. - Safety (soundness): if the token returns to the initiator white, then every process is passive and no messages are in transit (i.e., the system has actually terminated).
- Liveness (progress): if the system truly becomes quiescent (no active processes and no further messages are sent), then eventually the initiator will detect termination by receiving a white token.
- No false positives: the initiator must never conclude termination (declare termination) while some process is still active or some activation message is pending.
- Eventual detection under fair scheduling assumptions: assuming weak fairness of token-passing actions, termination will eventually be detected whenever it has occurred.

Parameterize the model by the ring size N, and state necessary assumptions (N ≥ 1). Do not prescribe an implementation; describe only state, permitted behaviors, and the correctness properties to be proven.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models the Paxos consensus algorithm, focusing on its safety properties and omitting explicit leader and learner processes. The model uses a message-passing abstraction, where the set of all messages ever sent is tracked, rather than modeling messages in transit or message loss. The specification includes a type invariant, an initial state, and a refinement mapping to a Voting module, as well as an inductive invariant for proof purposes. desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies the classic Paxos consensus algorithm as a message-passing system, without explicit leader or learner processes. It is instantiated with concrete constants: values `{1, 2}`, acceptors `{1, 2, 3}`, quorums `{{1,2},{2,3},{1,3}}`, and ballots `1..3`.

The state consists of four variables: `maxBal` (the highest ballot number each acceptor has promised to respect), `maxVBal` and `maxVal` (the ballot and value of each acceptor's highest-numbered vote), and `msgs` (the monotonically growing set of all messages ever sent). Four message types are modeled: phase-1a (ballot proposals), phase-1b (acceptor promises with their current vote state), phase-2a (leader value proposals), and phase-2b (acceptor votes).

The next-state relation comprises four actions. `Phase1a(b)` broadcasts a phase-1a message opening ballot `b`. `Phase1b(a)` allows acceptor `a` to respond to a phase-1a message whose ballot exceeds `maxBal[a]`, updating `maxBal[a]` and sending its prior vote information. `Phase2a(b,v)` allows a leader to propose value `v` in ballot `b` provided no phase-2a message for `b` exists yet and a quorum of phase-1b responses demonstrates that `v` is safe (either no prior votes exist in the quorum or the highest prior vote was for `v`). `Phase2b(a)` lets acceptor `a` vote for a proposed value if the proposal's ballot is at least `maxBal[a]`. The temporal specification is `Init ∧ [][Next]_vars` with no fairness conditions, targeting safety verification. The module defines an inductive invariant `Inv` asserting type correctness, consistency of per-acceptor vote records, and that every phase-2a message proposes a value shown safe by some quorum, supporting a refinement mapping to an abstract voting specification.
desc_intent:
Specify a fault-tolerant distributed consensus protocol based on classic Paxos (single-decree consensus) for a fixed set of acceptors and a finite set of ballot identifiers and proposal values. The model should describe message-based interactions between proposers (leaders) and acceptors, where proposers attempt ballots to get a value chosen and acceptors respond to prepare and accept requests. The specification must not commit to a particular leader-election mechanism; instead allow any proposer to initiate a ballot by broadcasting a prepare and then, after collecting responses from a quorum, to send an accept request for a value that is safe for that ballot.

The model must include:
- a representation of messages that can be sent (prepare, promise, accept-request, accepted) and the state that acceptors maintain (the highest promised ballot and any accepted ballot/value);
- nondeterministic message delivery (messages may be sent and later observed), but the safety properties are independent of losses;
- quorum-based decision making: a quorum is any set of acceptors satisfying pairwise intersection.

Key correctness properties:
- Safety (Agreement): At most one value can ever be chosen; once a value is chosen by a quorum of acceptors for some ballot, no different value can later be chosen in any other ballot.
- Integrity: Only values proposed by proposers can be chosen, and acceptors record only what they actually accepted.
- Promise monotonicity: once an acceptor promises not to accept below some ballot, it never accepts at a lower ballot.
- Validity of proposer choices: when a proposer issues an accept request for ballot b and value v, v must be consistent with the highest previously accepted values reported by a quorum during the prepare phase (i.e., v is either the highest accepted value among those responses or any value if none were accepted).

Additionally, specify an inductive invariant (state constraints) sufficient to prove safety, and state the initial conditions (no promises, no accepted values, no messages). Do not prescribe internal leader state or synchronous rounds beyond the abstract prepare/accept steps; model only messages and acceptor local state.

desc_intent:

desc_declarative_gpt: This module models an asynchronous Byzantine agreement protocol based on the Bracha-Toueg protocol, using counters for sent and received ECHO and READY messages together with per-process program counters.
