desc_intent: Specify a formal TLA+ model of the real numbers as a complete ordered field extended with two symbols representing positive and negative infinity, and of the usual arithmetic and order operations on them. The model should define a carrier set for the real numbers and provide operations for addition, multiplication, additive inverse, multiplicative inverse (on nonzero reals), subtraction, division, and exponentiation by integers and by nonnegative reals where defined. It must also define a total linear order on the extended line (reals plus ±infinity) that extends the usual ordering on reals and treats MinusInfinity as strictly less than every real and Infinity as strictly greater than every real. The model must enforce the field axioms for reals (associativity, commutativity, identities, inverses, distributivity), the Archimedean/Nat embedding property (natural numbers are represented and behave appropriately under successor), and the completeness axiom: every nonempty subset of reals that is bounded above has a least upper bound in the reals. Specify the behavior of arithmetic with infinities (e.g., comparisons, subtraction and division when operands include infinities) in a way that does not violate the field axioms on the real subset. Require existence of at least one structure satisfying these properties (a witness) and expose selectors to use the chosen structure in further specifications. State correctness properties to check: closure of operations on reals, preservation of order by addition and multiplication by nonnegative reals, existence and uniqueness conditions for inverses, and the completeness property for suprema.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module provides placeholder definitions for real-number-related operators rather than a full executable semantics. It models a dummy Reals module by defining a distinguished value Real, division as a CHOOSE-based operator over that value, and Infinity as a CHOOSE of an element outside Real that is greater than every element of Real. The file does not define a transition system, state variables, actions, temporal specification, fairness, or proofs; it is a mathematical support module intended for use by other specifications and tools.
desc_intent: Specify a formal model of a numeric system that augments the integers with a separate type of real-number-like values, supporting exact integer arithmetic, a distinct real value set, and mixed integer–real operations. The model should treat integer values and real values as disjoint domains and provide a well-defined binary division operation that accepts either two reals or two integers and returns a compatible numeric value; division by zero must be handled explicitly (e.g., by producing a distinguished Infinity value or by preventing the operation). Include a representation of an explicit Infinity element for the real side and rules for comparisons and arithmetic involving Infinity. The model must expose a notion of type discipline so that integer operations do not implicitly coerce integers into reals, yet mixed operations behave predictably according to specified promotion rules. Specify invariants ensuring preservation of integer arithmetic properties (associativity, commutativity for addition and multiplication, and identity elements) and correctness of mixed operations (no silent loss of integer identity, and deterministic promotion to real when required). State safety properties that forbid invalid divisions and operations across disjoint domains, and liveness properties guaranteeing that arithmetic computations progress when operands are valid. Include clear definitions of allowed values, division semantics, Infinity behavior, and required correctness invariants.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module defines standard operators for finite sequences in TLA+, representing a sequence of length n as a function with domain 1..n. It provides constructors and selectors such as Seq, Len, concatenation, Append, Head, Tail, SubSeq, and SelectSeq, with comments explaining their intended meaning and the representation of tuples as sequences. The module is a library-style definitions module rather than a transition-system specification: it declares no variables, no actions, and no temporal properties, and it notes that TLC overrides these operators with Java implementations.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal model of finite sequences (ordered lists) over an arbitrary element type and the operations and properties needed to manipulate them safely and predictably.

Model what a sequence is (a finite ordered collection with a well-defined length and indexed positions starting at 1) and provide these abstract operations: constructing the empty sequence and singleton sequences; obtaining the length; accessing the first element and the rest; concatenating two sequences; extracting a contiguous subsequence by start and end positions; appending an element; and selecting a subsequence by a predicate (filtering while preserving order).

Require the model to enforce standard invariants: lengths compose correctly under concatenation and appending; indices are valid only in the appropriate domain; head and tail are undefined for the empty sequence; subsequence extraction preserves element order and has length equal to n−m+1 for valid m≤n; concatenation and subsequence operations are associative and interact predictably (for example, extracting a contiguous range from a concatenation yields the appropriate pieces from each operand). For the filtering operation, require it to produce exactly those elements that satisfy the predicate in original order, and to be compositional (filtering with a conjunction equals successive filters). Specify boundary conditions and error conditions (e.g., invalid indices) as explicit side conditions. Include correctness properties that can be model-checked: preservation of element multiset under concatenation/append, idempotence where applicable, and invariants about domains and lengths.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module defines a grammar for the TLA+ language itself using grammar-combinator style operators imported from other modules. It defines lexical classes, operator-token classes, and a parameterized grammar operator P inside TLAPlusGrammar, then returns LeastGrammar(P). It is not a state-machine specification and contains no variables, actions, or temporal correctness properties.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal grammar-directed parser and validator for a rich specification language used to write concurrent and reactive system modules. The model should treat source text as a sequence of tokens and define the syntactic constructs that complete modules may contain: module headers and footers, import/extends lists, unit-level declarations (constants, variables, operator and function definitions, instances, module definitions), assumptions/axioms, theorems, and nested module bodies. It must support declarations of identifiers and reserved words, numeric and string literal forms, prefix/infix/postfix operator categories (including user-defined operator declarations), tuples and bracketed list forms, quantifiers and bounded quantification, choose/let/case constructs, set and sequence expressions, record and function expressions, EXCEPT updates, temporal operator applications, and the various expression compositions permitted by the language (including operator application, tuple formation, projections, and indexed expressions).

The specification must require that well-formed programs satisfy scoping and binding rules (identifiers are distinct from reserved words; operator and function definitions bind in their lexical scope; instance substitutions respect arity and operator kinds), enforce syntactic constraints on token sequences (e.g., required separators, matching delimiters, and minimum-length header/footer markers), and ensure construct-specific well-formedness (e.g., quantifier bounds must include a target expression, EXCEPT targets must be valid locations, and infix/prefix/postfix operator positions conform to declared forms). Specify key correctness properties: every accepted token sequence corresponds to exactly one abstract syntax tree (unambiguous parsing), all identifier uses are either declared or imported (no free undefined names), and the grammar is closed under composition of modules and instances (imports and substitutions preserve well-formedness).

desc_declarative_gpt: This module provides a TLAPS proof of type correctness for the Alternating Bit protocol, as specified in AlternatingBit.tla. The main theorem proved is that the specification ABSpec implies that the type invariant ABTypeInv always holds. The proof is structured hierarchically, with supporting lemmas establishing the type preservation of sequence operations such as Append, Tail, and Head, as well as the correctness of the Lose operation. The proof uses standard TLAPS commands and relies on the AlternatingBit and TLAPS modules for definitions and proof infrastructure.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal model of the Alternating Bit Protocol (ABP) for reliable message delivery over an unreliable channel. The model should represent a sender and a receiver that communicate by sending data messages and acknowledgments; messages may be lost but not corrupted or reordered. The sender transmits a stream of data values tagged with a one-bit sequence number; the receiver accepts each data item exactly once, delivers it in order, and returns an acknowledgment containing the corresponding bit. The sender retransmits the current message until it receives a matching acknowledgment, then advances to the next data item and toggles the bit. The receiver ignores duplicate data (same bit) but acknowledges it so the sender can stop retransmitting.

Require the specification to express:

- The state of sender and receiver (including current sequence bit and pending data) and the channel contents as sequences of messages and acknowledgments.
- A non-deterministic unreliable channel where send actions append messages and loss actions may remove an arbitrary message or acknowledgment.
- Safety properties: the channel only carries well-formed messages (bit paired with data), sent and received bits are within {0,1}, and type invariants for sequences are preserved by every transition.
- Liveness and correctness properties: every delivered data item is one of the sent data items in order, each data item is eventually delivered provided the sender stops sending new items and losses are fair, and no data item is delivered more than once.

Do not constrain timing or fairness beyond allowing nondeterministic loss; expose fairness assumptions needed to prove eventual delivery.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies the alternating bit protocol as a simple sender-receiver communication system with separate message and acknowledgment queues. The sender keeps a data value and a control bit, retransmits when an acknowledgment has not yet matched the current bit, and the receiver records the last received bit and data value while sending acknowledgments back. The environment may nondeterministically lose one element from either queue, and the specification checks a type invariant over the protocol state under a temporal specification with weak fairness for retransmission and acknowledgment sending and strong fairness for message and acknowledgment receipt.
desc_intent: Specify a formal model of a simple reliable data transfer protocol between a single sender and a single receiver that uses an alternating single-bit sequence number and acknowledgments to tolerate lossy, unordered channels. The model should describe the sender and receiver behaviors and the two unidirectional unreliable channels (data channel carrying (bit,message) pairs and acknowledgment channel carrying bits). The sender repeatedly accepts new application data items, transmits a packet that tags the data with the next sequence bit when it believes the previous packet was acknowledged, and retransmits the last packet when it suspects loss. The receiver accepts incoming packets, delivers data to the application only when the packet’s sequence bit matches the expected bit (thus avoiding duplicates), toggles its expected bit on successful delivery, and sends an acknowledgment message with the received bit. Both channels may nondeterministically drop individual messages but do not duplicate, reorder or corrupt message contents beyond loss. Specify fairness assumptions sufficient to ensure progress when messages and acknowledgments are eventually delivered often enough (e.g., weak fairness for retransmission and acknowledgment-sending actions and strong fairness for packet and ack receptions). Key correctness properties: safety—no delivered application data is ever corrupted and the receiver delivers each application datum at most once; and liveness—every datum that the sender attempts to send infinitely often (or is repeatedly retransmitted under fairness) is eventually delivered by the receiver and eventually acknowledged, assuming fair delivery conditions. Also assert an invariant capturing legal system states (types/domains of queues, bits, and data) and show it is preserved.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module defines a grammar for TLA+ configuration files using operators from the BNFGrammars module. It characterizes lexical classes such as letters, digits, identifiers, keywords, strings, and numbers, and then builds a grammar for configuration statements like SPECIFICATION, INIT, NEXT, VIEW, SYMMETRY, constraints, properties, constant replacements, and constant assignments. The specification is purely structural and declarative: it introduces no state variables, no transition actions, and no temporal correctness properties, but instead defines the accepted syntax of config files via grammar combinators and a LET-local grammar parameterized operator.
desc_intent: Specify a formal grammar and validator for a configuration-file language used to control a specification-checking tool. The model should capture the syntax of valid configuration files and enable automated checking of whether a given token sequence is a well-formed configuration. The configuration language must support: top-level statements that map a keyword to one or more identifiers; two classes of keywords—those that require exactly one identifier and those that allow zero or more identifiers; declaration sections for constants that can contain either assignments (name = value) or replacements (name <- identifier); identifiers composed of letters, underscores, and digits but not identical to reserved keywords; numeric values including optional leading minus; quoted string literals permitting a broad set of printable characters; and set-like value expressions using braces with comma-separated elements (including nested literal forms). The model should treat whitespace and token boundaries appropriately and allow repeated statements. Key correctness properties: (1) every accepted token sequence must unambiguously parse as a sequence of valid statements according to the grammar; (2) identifiers must be distinguished from reserved keywords; (3) numeric, string, and set literal forms must meet their lexical constraints; (4) replacements and assignments are only allowed inside constant-declaration statements; (5) the grammar is the least (smallest) grammar satisfying these rules (no extra productions). Provide enough structure to generate or validate example token sequences and to check these invariants.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a state-graph exploration algorithm that searches a directed graph represented as a record with components `states`, `initials`, and `actions`. The explorer does not enforce BFS ordering: the frontier `S` is a set, and the next state to explore is chosen non-deterministically, while it still records predecessor edges and level information to reconstruct a counterexample path. It checks for safety violations and deadlocks, reconstructs a path once termination is detected, and asserts temporal properties for overall termination and for eventual discovery of a violation state together with a valid counterexample path, under weak fairness of `Next`.
desc_intent:
Specify a model of a graph state-space explorer that searches a directed state graph to detect safety violations or dead ends and, when found, produces a concrete path (counterexample) from an initial state to the offending state. The model should treat the set of graph states and the transition relation abstractly: the graph is given by a finite set of states, a designated subset of initial states, and a successor function that maps every state to a set of next states.

The explorer must maintain an explicit notion of which states have been discovered and which remain to be explored (a frontier), allow nondeterministic choice of which frontier state to expand next (no enforced BFS ordering), and record a spanning relation that associates every newly discovered state with a predecessor so that full paths can be reconstructed. Exploration of a state must add all of its previously unvisited successors to the frontier and record predecessor links; if a state has no successors, that must be detected as a dead end.

The model must detect two stopping conditions: reaching a state that belongs to a designated set of violation states, and reaching a dead-end state. Upon detecting either, it must mark exploration as finished and construct a finite sequence of states representing a path from some initial state to the detected state by following predecessor links backward. Key correctness properties to specify and prove are: safety (if a constructed counterexample ends in a violation or dead end, every adjacent pair in the path is a valid transition in the graph and the first state is initial), liveness (if any violation state exists then eventually a violation is found and a valid counterexample produced), and termination (the procedure eventually halts when either a violation is found or the frontier and pending successors are exhausted). Also require that the explorer never revisits a state as “unvisited” after it has been marked discovered.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module defines a collection of directed state graphs together with associated violation sets and example counterexample paths, intended for testing model-checker specifications such as TLCMC and MCReachability. Each graph is represented as a record with fields for the set of states, the set of initial states, and a sequence of successor-state sets indexed by state number; separate operators define the corresponding violating states and witness traces. The module contains no variables, actions, temporal specification, fairness, or proofs; instead it serves as a static data library that selects one named test case based on the IO environment variable GRAPH, defaulting to graph 7 when that setting is absent.
desc_intent:
Specify a model of directed finite-state graphs used to represent transition systems, and a tool that analyzes reachability and counterexample extraction. The model should allow an arbitrary directed graph with a finite set of nodes, a distinguished set of initial nodes, and a collection of labeled transitions where each transition from a node can nondeterministically lead to one of several successor nodes (including none). The system to specify must support the following analyses and guarantees:

- Reachability: determine which nodes are reachable from the initial set via zero or more transitions.
- Violation detection: given a set of designated "bad" nodes, determine whether any bad node is reachable.
- Counterexample generation: when a bad node is reachable, provide at least one finite path (sequence of nodes starting in an initial node) that leads to a bad node.
- Support for multiple independent test graphs: the specification must be parametric so different graphs, initial sets, transition collections, and bad-node sets can be plugged in.
- Correctness properties: (1) any returned counterexample is a valid path consistent with the graph’s transitions and starts at an initial node and ends at a bad node; (2) if no counterexample is returned the model must guarantee that no bad node is reachable; (3) reachability computation must be sound and complete relative to finite path semantics.
- Edge cases: handle empty graphs, nodes with no outgoing transitions, multi-sink structures, and graphs with strongly connected components.

Do not prescribe any particular algorithmic implementation; state only the required semantics, outputs, and correctness obligations.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module models a TLC-like reachability model checker that performs breadth-first exploration over a graph of states, with a parameter K controlling whether exploration is strict BFS (K = 1) or degraded non-strict BFS (K > 1) to approximate multiple workers. The state graph is given as a record with states, initial states, and an action relation, and the model checker tracks explored states, a queue of pending states, predecessor information, and BFS levels in order to detect violations and reconstruct counterexamples. The specification verifies termination of the translated PlusCal algorithm and a liveness-style property stating that when violation states exist, the eventual counterexample belongs to a supplied set of known counterexamples, with an additional minimal-length requirement when K = 1; it also includes a refinement mapping to an instantiated MCReachability specification.
desc_intent:
Specify a model of a breadth‑first state‑space exploration algorithm that searches a directed state graph for violation states and returns a shortest counterexample path when one exists. The system should accept as input: a finite directed graph with a set of initial states and a set of target (violation) states; a predicate that can prune states depending on their BFS level; a configurable parallelism/window parameter K that controls how many of the next queued states may be chosen for expansion at each step; and a (possibly empty) set of known counterexample sequences for liveness reasoning.

The model must describe exploration semantics (not an implementation): new states are discovered by following transitions from explored states, constrained by the pruning predicate so that successors for which the predicate is false are not enqueued or recorded. Initial states may be explored in any order, and the queue ordering of unexplored states should be represented such that when K = 1 the algorithm always dequeues the head (strict BFS), while K > 1 allows nondeterministic dequeueing among the first min(K, queue length) positions (modeling parallel workers and degraded strictness). Detect and report a counterexample when an initial state or any discovered successor is a violation state, producing a concrete path from some initial state to that violation. Also detect deadlock states (no outgoing transitions except self‑loop) and report them as counterexamples.

Specify correctness properties:
- Safety: any reported counterexample is a valid path in the input graph from an initial state to a violation or deadlock.
- BFS minimality: when K = 1 and the pruning predicate does not remove states on a shortest path, any reported counterexample has minimum length among all reachable violation paths.
- Completeness modulo pruning: if a violation is reachable through states that satisfy the pruning predicate, the algorithm eventually reports some such violation (if the model is fair).
- Termination: if no reachable violation remains (modulo pruning), the exploration terminates with the queue empty.
- Liveness: if a set of known counterexamples is provided, the model should permit the algorithm to eventually stabilize on producing one of those counterexamples; when K = 1, the chosen counterexample should have minimal length among that set.

Do not encode implementation details such as explicit queue removal indices or pair encoding; abstractly model queue semantics, explored set, predecessor information sufficient to reconstruct reported paths, and the nondeterministic dequeue choice constrained by K.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module provides wrapper theorems that expose TypeOK and Inv as named invariants of the Spec for the SimpleRegular algorithm. The actual inductive content and algorithmic details are contained in the imported SimpleRegular module; this file focuses on stating and proving that TypeOK and Inv are invariants under the system's specification. The proofs are structured hierarchically and use TLAPS proof constructs, but do not introduce new algorithmic content or state variables. The design is intended for proof management and clarity, making the invariants explicit for use in further verification or as proof obligations.
desc_intent:
Specify a parameterized distributed protocol in which N identical processes are arranged in a logical ring and repeatedly perform a local read-modify-write protocol on shared arrays. The system must model that each process can be in a finite set of control states and that processes take atomic steps that may read from one process’s buffer and write into its own slot. The model must capture asynchronous interleaving: at each step one process executes a single enabled action. Actions include local initiation, a two-phase update that reads a value produced by the predecessor in the ring and then installs a value into the process’s own entry, and a termination step. The protocol must ensure type safety (all state components always have values of the intended domains) and must maintain a global inductive invariant that captures the intended relation between the ring buffers and process control states.

Formalize safety properties:
- Every reachable state satisfies the type constraints on all variables.
- A specified invariant holds initially and is preserved by every atomic step.
- Once a process reaches its terminal control state it remains terminated and cannot violate the invariant.

Specify the initial condition, nondeterministic choices for actions, and the transition relation abstractly (without prescribing implementation order beyond atomicity). State liveness only minimally: the system is terminating in the sense that behavior respects the termination action. Provide the invariant to be proved and state which properties must be discharged by model checking or theorem proving.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module provides wrapper theorems that expose TypeOK and Inv as named invariants of the Spec specification. The actual inductive content and system model are defined in the imported Simple module, specifically in its Correctness property. The theorems here formally state that Spec implies the invariance of TypeOK and Inv, and provide structured proofs using TLAPS proof steps. No algorithm or system is directly modeled in this file; instead, it serves as a proof harness for properties defined elsewhere.
desc_intent:
Model a simple concurrent program with a fixed set of identical processes that repeatedly perform an action until they terminate. The system must initialize with each process in a defined starting state and with global data satisfying given type and range constraints. Each process may non-deterministically perform a local step that updates only its own local state and possibly some shared variables; steps must preserve type and range invariants and may change a per-process termination flag. Processes do not create or destroy other processes.

Specify a safety invariant that is always preserved: a global predicate asserting well-typedness and bounds of all variables and a per-process invariant that constrains the relationship between a process’s local state, its termination status, and any shared variables. The specification must prove that (1) the initialization implies the per-process invariant, (2) any single step by any process, or stuttering of the system, preserves that invariant, and (3) the invariant implies the global type-and-range property.

Also specify liveness: every non-terminated process that is enabled infinitely often eventually takes a step (weak fairness). Ensure the model captures stuttering steps and uses a standard next-state relation for either a single-process step or stuttering. The correctness properties to guarantee are safety (the per-process invariant and global type invariants hold always) and the stated fairness liveness condition.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a simple alternating system with two state variables, v and x. The variable v acts as a control bit that alternates between 0 and 1, and each transition corresponds to one of two abstract actions: an A_0 action when v changes from 0 to 1, and an A_1 action when v changes from 1 to 0. The details of x's initial value and transition behavior are abstracted by the operator-valued constants XInit and XAct, and the temporal property Spec requires the system to start in Init and then always take Next steps.
desc_intent:
Specify a system that repeatedly alternates between two distinct kinds of state updates, called action A0 and action A1. The system maintains a control token that enforces strict alternation: each step must perform the other action from the one performed in the previous step. On startup the control token is set so that A0 is the first action to occur. The system also maintains an auxiliary payload component that represents the application state modified by A0 and A1. Each occurrence of A0 must transform the payload from a value satisfying the valid precondition for A0 to a value satisfying the valid postcondition for A0; likewise each occurrence of A1 must transform the payload from a value satisfying the valid precondition for A1 to a value satisfying the valid postcondition for A1. The initial state must satisfy the payload’s allowed initial condition.

Model the system as a discrete-state transition system with nonblocking progress: from any state where the control token indicates the next action, there must exist at least one legal transition implementing that indicated action and updating the payload accordingly. Require safety properties: the control token must always alternate and the payload transitions must always conform to the action-specific correctness relation. Require liveness: both A0 and A1 occur infinitely often (no permanent starvation). The specification should abstract the concrete payload semantics by parameterizing initial and action-correctness predicates so different payload models can be substituted.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies the two-phase handshake protocol, a fundamental hardware protocol involving a Producer and a Consumer process that alternate actions, with the Producer acting first. The protocol is modeled with variables representing the state of the Producer (p), Consumer (c), and an abstract data variable (x), with actions for each process and a temporal specification ensuring alternation. The module also demonstrates that this protocol implements the Alternate specification under a refinement mapping, using a function vBar to relate the two, and provides a detailed TLAPS proof of this implementation.
desc_intent:
Specify a model of a two-party alternation protocol in which a Producer and a Consumer take turns performing actions, with the Producer always going first. The system should include a shared state component representing some payload or data value that both parties may read and update when they act. The protocol must enforce that at any given time exactly one party is enabled to perform its action: when the parties are synchronized in phase, the Producer is enabled; after the Producer acts, the Consumer becomes enabled; after the Consumer acts, the Producer becomes enabled again, and so on, alternating indefinitely.

Model the initial condition, the allowed actions of each party on the shared payload (abstracting the payload update as a parameterized relation), and the handshaking control that ensures strict alternation. The model should allow the payload update relation to be any relation satisfying an initialization predicate and per-step transition relation so proofs about control flow do not depend on a concrete payload implementation.

State the safety properties: the control variables always remain within the two permitted phases, and the alternation invariant that exactly one of the two actions is enabled at each step and the roles alternate after each action. Also specify a refinement property: show that the two-party handshaking system implements an abstract alternating-binary-state specification by mapping the concrete control state to a single abstract bit that toggles on every action. Include liveness goals that the system can always make progress (no deadlock) assuming the payload relation allows the corresponding party to perform its update.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies the Yo-Yo leader election algorithm on arbitrary strongly connected undirected graphs without self-loops, where nodes are identified by integers and the node with the smallest identifier is the eventual leader. The algorithm maintains an orientation of graph edges via incoming and outgoing neighbor sets and alternates between a down phase, where minimum identifiers are propagated toward sinks, and an up phase, where yes/no replies propagate back and edges receiving a "no" are reversed. The specification models asynchronous node steps as a state machine, assumes a strongly connected undirected input graph, and verifies type correctness, structural neighbor consistency, absence of newly created sources, and eventual stabilization to a state where only the minimum node remains the unique source and all up messages are "yes".
desc_intent:
Specify a formal TLA+ model of the Yo‑Yo leader‑election algorithm running on an arbitrary undirected, connected graph of distinct integer‑identified nodes. The model should describe rounds composed of two phases ("down" then "up") that propagate candidate identities along oriented edges and that may reverse edge orientations based on comparisons, with the global objective that the node with the smallest identifier becomes the unique leader candidate. The system must allow asynchronous interleaving of local actions at nodes, message passing via per‑node mailboxes, and nondeterministic scheduling, but assume reliable delivery and that each round’s messages are processed before that node advances to the next phase.

Requirements:
- Initialization: every undirected edge has an initial orientation determined by node identifiers (smaller -> larger), and every node starts the down phase with empty mailboxes.
- Down phase semantics: sources (local minima) broadcast their identity; non‑sources wait to receive values from all incoming neighbors and forward the minimum seen to their outgoing neighbors; sinks do not send in the down phase.
- Up phase semantics: sinks reply to neighbors that sent the round’s minimum with "yes" and to others with "no"; intermediate nodes collect replies from outgoing neighbors, propagate "no" if any outgoing reply is "no", otherwise reply "yes" only to incoming neighbors that contributed the minimum; sources do not send in the up phase.
- Edge reversal: an edge must change orientation whenever a "no" is sent along it during the up phase; mailboxes must accurately reflect messages in flight during orientation changes so that reversals are observable.
- Safety properties to verify: preservation of message/neighbor consistency during reversals (a relation between incoming/outgoing sets and pending "no" messages), no creation of new sources beyond those due to reversals, and eventual uniqueness of the smallest‑id source.
- Liveness property: the algorithm stabilizes with exactly one source (the node with minimal id), after which all down messages carry that id and all up replies are "yes" forever (stabilization eventually holds).

Do not embed pruning or explicit termination detection in the primary model; instead ensure the specification can be extended to add pruning as a separate variant.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models the Yo-Yo leader-election algorithm on a strongly connected undirected graph, extended with pruning so that the algorithm terminates. Nodes alternate between down and up phases, exchange structured messages through mailboxes, reverse or prune edges based on replies, and eventually eliminate all but one source so that the smallest node becomes an isolated leader. The spec assumes a connected undirected graph, uses weak fairness for the main next-state action, and states both safety-style properties about graph consistency and termination-style temporal properties such as eventual termination and equivalence between deadlock and the terminated condition.
desc_intent:
Specify a TLA+ model of a distributed leader election algorithm that runs on an undirected, connected graph of uniquely identified nodes and guarantees eventual election of a single leader with termination detection. Model nodes that communicate only with neighbors by asynchronous message passing in rounds that alternate a "down" phase and an "up" phase. The protocol must propagate candidate identifiers outward during the down phase and aggregate responses during the up phase so that smaller identifiers win ties. To ensure progress and termination, include pruning rules in the up phase that (a) allow a sink node with only one incoming neighbor to become inactive and be removed, and (b) allow a node that received the same value from multiple incoming neighbors to non-deterministically keep exactly one incoming link for each distinct value while removing the other equivalent incoming links. Pruning actions must be signaled in messages so receivers can update local neighbor sets consistently even with in-flight messages.

Require invariants that maintain that every message references currently adjacent nodes except as allowed for in-flight reversals or pruning, that node kinds (source/ internal/ sink/ leader) are determined by incoming/outgoing neighbor sets, and that no mailbox contains more than one message per (phase, sender) pair. Specify correctness properties: eventual termination in a state where exactly one node (the minimum id) is isolated and declared leader, all other nodes are inactive, and all mailboxes are empty; safety properties preventing multiple leaders; and a formulation relating enabled transitions to termination (deadlock iff termination). Include liveness that the system eventually reaches the termination state.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a non-blocking atomic commitment protocol variant in which reliable broadcast is used to obtain the non-blocking property. It extends a base module for atomic commitment and adds participant forwarding state so that when a participant receives a decision, it forwards that decision to all other participants before locally delivering it. The specification defines participant-side actions for forwarding, pre-deciding from forwarded or coordinator messages, deciding after forwarding is complete, and aborting on simulated timeout conditions, then combines them into a temporal specification with weak fairness assumptions and includes some invalid liveness-style properties such as all-commit, all-abort, and a yes-votes leads-to commit condition.
desc_intent:
Model a nonblocking atomic commitment protocol for a distributed transaction coordinator and N participants. The model should describe the allowed behaviors of the coordinator and of each participant abstractly (not an implementation), and must capture the message dissemination, fault, and timing assumptions needed to guarantee safety and liveness.

Requirements:

- The coordinator collects votes (yes/no) from participants and decides commit only if every live participant voted yes; otherwise it can decide abort. The coordinator may be faulty (crash-stop) and may fail to deliver its decision to some participants.

- Participants may crash (crash-stop) and recover is not required. Participants forward received decisions to other participants using a reliable forwarding mechanism so that a decision delivered anywhere can be propagated to all live participants without relying on the original sender. Forwarding should be reliable in the sense that an alive participant that has a decision can send it to an alive peer; messages are not lost between alive processes.

- Nonblocking liveness: if a majority (or more generally, all live) participants are alive and the coordinator is dead or unreachable, the protocol must allow live participants to reach a decision (commit or abort) without waiting indefinitely for the coordinator, using forwarded decisions.

- Safety (agreement): No two non-faulty participants decide differently (no conflicting commit/abort among alive participants). Also, the protocol must satisfy validity: if all participants voted yes and the coordinator is non-faulty, then non-faulty participants may only decide commit; if any vote is no, then commit must not be decided by any non-faulty participant.

- Progress: Under fair scheduling and the reliable forwarding assumption, every live non-faulty participant eventually decides (either commit or abort). The model should express termination under the assumed liveness conditions (e.g., coordinator alive and broadcasts, or forwarding among live participants).

Specify the system as an asynchronous, message-passing distributed protocol with explicit abstractions for votes, coordinator decision broadcasts, per-participant storage of received decisions, forwarding of decisions between participants, crash failures, and fairness assumptions sufficient to state and verify the above safety and liveness properties.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies an atomic commitment protocol with one coordinator and a set of participants, using a simple broadcast mechanism in an asynchronous setting. The comments explain that synchronous communication has been replaced by implicit asynchronous communication and that failures are detected magically rather than via timeouts; because broadcast is modeled as a sequence of individual sends that can be interrupted by failure, the protocol is non-terminating and the usual termination property AC5 does not hold. The specification defines typed initial states, participant and coordinator actions, a next-state relation with weak fairness on non-death progress actions, and then states safety, liveness, stronger auxiliary properties, and explicitly invalid properties for the protocol.
desc_intent:
Specify a TLA+ model of a non‑blocking atomic commitment protocol for one coordinator and a set of participants that communicate by unreliable asynchronous point‑to‑point messages and by a simple broadcast primitive (a broadcast is modeled as sending the same message individually to each participant, any of which may be lost if the sender or a recipient fails). The model should represent crashes (stop failures) of the coordinator and participants; a crashed process stays crashed. Failures may be detected by other processes (modeled abstractly, not by real timeouts), and message loss may occur due to crashes during send.

The protocol to be modeled is the classic two‑phase style atomic commitment where:
- The coordinator first requests votes from all participants.
- Each live participant that receives a request replies with a vote (yes or no).
- The coordinator collects votes (unless some participant crashes or its vote is not delivered) and decides: commit iff all collected votes are yes, otherwise abort.
- The coordinator broadcasts its decision to participants using the simple broadcast primitive; participants that receive the decision adopt it.
- Participants may also decide locally to abort if they observe failures that prevent safe commit (e.g., coordinator crashed before sending request or a participant voted no).

Specify initial conditions and legal state space (who is alive, votes, undecided/commit/abort decisions). State the allowed transitions abstractly (sending requests, sending votes, coordinator making decision, broadcasting decision, process crashes) but do not prescribe implementation sequencing.

Require and formalize safety properties:
- Agreement: no two non‑faulty participants decide differently; once a participant decides, its decision does not change.
- Validity: commit can occur only if every participant’s vote was yes.
- Abort justification: an abort decision must be explainable by at least one no vote or by some crash (participant or coordinator).

Require liveness properties under appropriate fairness and fault assumptions:
- If no failures occur thereafter, all live participants eventually decide.
- If the coordinator and all participants remain non‑faulty and messages eventually get through, the protocol terminates with every participant deciding (commit or abort) consistent with validity.

Also include auxiliary invariants to aid reasoning (e.g., stability of faults and votes) but do not tie the specification to a particular implementation or variable naming.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module contains TLAPS proofs for two safety properties of the SimpleAllocator specification: that SimpleAllocator implies the invariants TypeInvariant and ResourceMutex. TypeInvariant is shown to be directly inductive, while ResourceMutex requires the combined invariant Inv (TypeInvariant and ResourceMutex) and an argument about the disjointness of allocated resources. The proofs are fully written in hierarchical style, with detailed reasoning about each action (Request, Allocate, Return) and the preservation of invariants. The module does not define the allocator algorithm itself, but proves properties about it using definitions and actions from the imported SimpleAllocator module.
desc_intent:
Specify a concurrent resource allocator for a fixed finite set of clients and a fixed finite set of resources. The system should manage which resources are currently available and which subsets of resources are allocated to each client. Clients may issue three kinds of operations: request a subset of resources, receive an allocation of some subset (only from currently available resources), and return a subset of resources they hold. The allocator must ensure that allocations only assign resources that are available at the time of allocation, and that when a client receives resources those resources are removed from the available pool until returned. Returning resources must put them back into the available pool.

Model the system as an asynchronous discrete transition system where at each step one client may perform one of the operations; the model should allow arbitrary interleavings but enforce that operations respect set membership (clients and resources) and that only legal allocations are performed.

Specify and prove the following safety properties:

- Type invariants: the state always respects domain and range typing (e.g., available is a subset of resources; every client's held set is a subset of resources; allocations are tracked for all clients).

- Mutual exclusion of resources: at all times, the sets of resources held by distinct clients are pairwise disjoint (no resource is simultaneously held by two clients).

Also require that the allocation operation preserves the mutual-exclusion invariant (i.e., allocations are drawn only from currently available resources so they cannot create overlaps). Do not require liveness properties.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module provides a TLAPS proof for the VoucherLifeCycle specification, specifically proving that the temporal property VSpec implies that the invariants VTypeOK and VConsistent always hold. The proof demonstrates that these two invariants together form an inductive invariant for the system. The proof is structured hierarchically and references the underlying system's initialization and next-state actions, but does not introduce new algorithmic behavior or fault models.
desc_intent: Specify a formal TLA+ model of a voucher lifecycle management system used by an issuer and multiple holders. The model should describe vouchers as identifiable tokens that may be created, transferred among accounts, redeemed for value, or cancelled. It must allow concurrent operations by different principals and model eventual termination of a voucher’s active lifecycle (either redeemed or cancelled). The system must enforce type and structural invariants: every voucher has a unique identifier, a valid owner (an authorized account or a special null owner when not assigned), a nonnegative remaining value, and a well-defined state drawn from a fixed set of lifecycle states (e.g., issued, active, redeemed, cancelled). Operations must only apply when preconditions hold (for example, only the issuer may create vouchers; only current owner may transfer; redemption requires sufficient remaining value and appropriate state). Safety properties to guarantee: uniqueness of identifiers, preservation of total supply accounting (no creation or destruction of value except by authorized issuance and redemption), absence of double redemption (a voucher cannot be redeemed twice), and ownership-consistency (the recorded owner matches transfers). Liveness properties to guarantee: issued vouchers that remain active can eventually be redeemed or cancelled under fair scheduling assumptions, and transfers do not deadlock progress of other independent vouchers. Specify these as invariants and temporal properties (safety as invariants; liveness as eventualities) suitable for model checking and theorem proving.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a crash-prone conditional consensus protocol in which processes exchange two phases of broadcast messages and use the maximal proposed value to drive decisions. The fault model is crash failures: up to F processes may crash, and crashed processes stop taking protocol steps. The spec defines initialization, message reception, both broadcast phases, local decision steps, and a deterministic fallback choose step, and it verifies typing, validity, agreement, unconditional termination as a temporal property, and a stronger conditional termination result under Condition1.
desc_intent:
Model a fault-tolerant consensus protocol among N processes that uses a two-phase broadcast to try to agree on a value equal to the maximum of proposed inputs when a particular condition holds. The model should capture asynchronous message sending and reception, crash faults (up to F faulty processes), and the following high-level behavior: in phase one, each noncrashed process broadcasts its input; after receiving sufficiently many phase‑one messages, it computes a local estimate based on the maximal value seen; in phase two, processes broadcast their estimates along with the value they expect others to have; upon collecting sufficiently many phase‑two messages, a process either decides a value that is supported by a large quorum or, if it has heard from every process, deterministically chooses a value from its view. The specification must permit processes to crash at any time, limited by the bound F, and must model unreliable delivery only insofar as messages can be delayed but not forged.

Require the following correctness properties to be specified and checked:
- Validity: any decided value must equal some process’s original input.
- Agreement: no two noncrashed processes decide different values.
- Termination: under the protocol’s condition that more than F processes propose the global maximum input, every noncrashed process eventually decides.
Also specify safety/typing invariants for message and state formats and ensure liveness assumptions that allow processes to eventually receive the needed quorums of messages unless crashed.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies the Chang-Roberts leader election algorithm on a unidirectional ring of N nodes, where each node has a unique natural-number identity given by the sequence Id. The embedded comments explain that any subset of nodes may initiate the algorithm, and the node with the smallest identity is intended to be elected leader. The specification includes a PlusCal algorithm and its TLA+ translation, defines type correctness and a safety correctness condition about the winner and losing nodes, and states a liveness property that if some candidate exists then eventually some node wins. The temporal specification uses weak fairness for every process action and allows infinite stuttering through a Terminating action to avoid deadlock on termination.
desc_intent:
Specify a model of the Chang–Roberts leader election algorithm running on a unidirectional ring of N deterministic processes with unique numeric identities. The model should allow any subset of processes to initiate the election concurrently by sending their own identity as a candidate message to their clockwise neighbor. Processes forward candidate messages, compare incoming candidate IDs with their own identity, and withdraw candidacy when they receive a smaller ID; when a process receives its own ID back, it declares itself leader.

Abstract the communication as asynchronous message delivery on the ring (messages may be in transit and can be buffered per recipient). Do not fix message ordering beyond per-recipient buffering. Model process state only in terms of whether it is currently a candidate, has lost, or has won, and the messages pending for each process. Allow all processes to run fairly.

Require the following correctness properties:
- Safety: If a process declares itself leader, it must have been an initiator and must hold the globally smallest identity among initiators; all other processes must have the “lost” status at that point.
- Uniqueness: At most one process may ever declare itself leader.
- Termination/Liveness: If at least one initiator exists, eventually some process declares itself leader.
- Progress fairness: Under weak fairness for each process step, election completes (no livelock).

Parameterize the model by N and the sequence of unique process identities. Provide invariants and temporal properties expressing the above safety, uniqueness, and liveness requirements, but do not prescribe a particular implementation encoding.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module defines helper notions on directed acyclic graphs for DAG-based consensus protocols, focusing on vertices that are pairs of a network node and a round. It defines leader vertices, a deterministic-but-arbitrary ordering of set elements, a way to find the previous leader in a DAG, and a recursive linearization procedure that turns a DAG into a sequence. The specification is not itself a full transition-system protocol model with variables and actions; instead it provides structural functions and predicates intended to support safety and liveness reasoning about DAG-based consensus, assuming a genesis vertex and that DAG paths terminate at genesis.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal model of a block-DAG based distributed ledger used by a set of network nodes that repeatedly propose blocks in discrete rounds under rotating leadership. The model should treat blocks as lightweight records that identify their proposer and the round they were created in, and should include a distinguished genesis block. Describe how each honest node accumulates a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of blocks by adding blocks that may reference prior blocks, so that every DAG contains the genesis block and every path ends at genesis.

The model must provide a deterministic method to extract a linear sequence of blocks from any DAG that is consistent across honest nodes when their DAGs sufficiently overlap: it may use an arbitrary but deterministic ordering of a DAG’s vertices that respects the DAG structure in that earlier leaders’ blocks appear before later leaders’ blocks. Define a notion of a leader block for each round and a way to locate the most recent leader block before a given round inside a DAG.

Specify safety and liveness properties to verify:

- Safety (Agreement): If two honest nodes produce linearizations from DAGs that both contain the same leader blocks up to some round, then those linearizations must be compatible (one is a prefix of the other).
- Liveness (Progress): If honest leaders keep proposing blocks and honest nodes eventually receive those blocks, then the extracted linearization grows (new blocks become finalizable/visible in the sequence).
- Integrity: Extracted sequences contain only blocks that are present in the node’s DAG and include genesis exactly once.

Do not prescribe a particular implementation of message delays, failure model, or ordering beyond the deterministic tie-breaking; allow parametrization of the set of nodes, rounds, and leader assignment.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module defines a directed graph abstraction represented as a pair consisting of a set of vertices and a set of edges. It provides operators to project the vertex and edge components, check whether a value is a well-formed digraph, compute the children of a vertex, compute the descendants reachable from a set of vertices using a recursive definition, and construct the reachable subgraph induced by a starting set of vertices. The module contains no variables, actions, temporal specification, fairness conditions, PlusCal algorithm, or proofs; it is a purely structural and recursive helper module for reasoning about directed graphs.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal model of a finite directed graph and operations that compute reachability and induce subgraphs, together with correctness properties about those computations.

Model a directed graph as a pair of a finite set of vertices and a set of ordered edges between vertices. Provide an operation that, given a set of start vertices, computes the set of all vertices reachable from that set via zero or more directed edge traversals. Provide an operation that, given a set of start vertices, produces the subgraph induced by all vertices reachable from those starts (i.e., the reachable vertices together with all edges whose source is a reachable vertex). Ensure the model makes no assumptions about acyclicity: reachability must behave correctly in the presence of cycles.

Require and prove the following properties:
- Safety: every vertex in the reachable set is indeed a vertex of the original graph, and every edge in the induced subgraph is an edge of the original graph whose source is in the reachable set.
- Correctness of reachability closure: the reachable set is the least set containing the start vertices and closed under taking direct successors (i.e., if a vertex is reachable then all its immediate children along outgoing edges from any reachable vertex are also reachable).
- Termination (for finite graphs): the reachability computation stabilizes in a finite number of steps and yields a fixed point.
- Idempotence of subgraph extraction: extracting the induced subgraph from an induced subgraph yields the same subgraph.
- Consistency: if the start set is empty, the reachable set is empty and the induced subgraph has no vertices or edges.

Include well-formedness invariants for graphs (edges connect existing vertices and are ordered pairs) and state all properties as invariants or theorems to be checked.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module gives a high-level TLA+ specification of the Sailfish and Sailfish++ consensus algorithms, modeling a DAG-based protocol with correct and Byzantine nodes. The comments explain that Byzantine behavior is constrained because vertices are disseminated with reliable broadcast, so Byzantine nodes cannot equivocate and can only create protocol-conforming vertices subject to quorum checks. The specification defines initialization, the next-state relation for correct and Byzantine nodes, a basic type invariant, an agreement safety property over delivered logs, and a liveness property stating that after GST, leaders of synchronous rounds are eventually reflected in correct nodes' logs.
desc_intent:
Specify a high-level model of a round-based leader-driven Byzantine fault-tolerant replication protocol that builds a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of proposals and uses quorum-based voting to decide and linearize committed proposals. The model should treat nodes partitioned into correct and Byzantine, and rounds numbered starting at 1 with a distinguished leader for each round. Correct nodes repeatedly participate in rounds by proposing a vertex that references a quorum of vertices from the previous round; correct proposals must reference only vertices from the immediately prior round. Byzantine nodes may also propose vertices but may not equivocate (a node cannot create two different vertices for the same round). Message delivery and proposal dissemination are abstracted: a proposal becomes visible to a node when that node includes it among a selected quorum of previous-round vertices.

The specification must capture these requirements and correctness properties:

- Safety (Agreement): All correct nodes must always produce compatible linearized logs — once a node has produced a log prefix, every other correct node’s log must be compatible with it (no two correct nodes produce conflicting committed sequences).

- Validity of DAG structure: Every vertex must be attributed to a valid node and round; children of a vertex must belong to exactly the previous round; edges connect existing vertices.

- Quorum and blocking semantics: Define quorums and blocking sets abstractly so that quorums ensure progress and blocking sets capture sufficient evidence that a leader cannot be committed.

- Liveness under partial synchrony: After a global stabilization time, if a round’s leader is correct, then every sufficiently advanced correct node (at least two rounds ahead) eventually has the leader’s vertex included and therefore the leader’s proposal can become committed and appear in its log.

- Non-equivocation constraint: Byzantine nodes cannot create two different vertices for the same round; their proposals are only considered by correct nodes when quorum conditions are met.

Do not prescribe an implementation mechanism (no concrete broadcast or timers); instead specify the invariants and temporal properties that ensure safety and eventual liveness given the quorum and blocking assumptions.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module defines a small collection of utility operators for use by other specifications. It provides a generic reduction operator over an integer interval, simple arithmetic aggregation, sequence membership and removal helpers, a function range constructor, and a predicate for detecting whether a function induces a simple cycle over a finite set. The module is purely definitional: it declares no variables, no transition actions, and no temporal specification or fault model.
desc_intent:
Specify a small utility library for manipulating finite nonempty sets of integers that will be used by other TLA+ specifications. The model should define the abstract operations of computing the maximum and minimum element of a nonempty finite integer set, and must state their expected behavior and properties without prescribing a particular implementation technique.

The specification must require that the max operation always returns an element of the input set and that every other element of the set is less than or equal to the returned element. Symmetrically, the min operation must always return an element of the input set and every other element must be greater than or equal to the returned element. Both operations must be total on the domain of finite nonempty integer sets and must be undefined (or explicitly disallowed) on empty sets.

Include simple algebraic properties necessary for compositional reasoning: idempotence when applied twice yields the same element, invariance under singleton sets, and monotonicity under subset relationships where the subset remains nonempty (for example, the max of a subset is less than or equal to the max of its superset). State that these operators commute with integer translation (adding a constant to every element shifts the result by that constant) and respect negation symmetry between max and min. Also assert basic correctness lemmas useful for proofs that use these utilities.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies an age-aware message channel in which messages are wrapped into boxes that carry both the original message content and an integer-valued transit age. The state tracks the set of boxed messages currently in transit and the set of messages delivered in the current transition, with actions for picking up new messages, delivering a nondeterministically chosen subset addressed to a given receiver, and advancing the age of all in-transit boxes. The specification includes initialization and a type invariant, but it does not define a full temporal specification such as Spec, fairness, or liveness properties; it focuses on the state representation and transition-level behavior of the channel.
desc_intent:
Specify a formally verified model of a message-passing channel with bounded-state descriptions of message transit and delivery. The model should capture the following system and requirements without prescribing internal implementation details:

- System: a communication substrate that carries discrete messages from senders to receivers by placing each message into a packet-like container that records how long the message has been in transit. The substrate supports three kinds of observable events: sending (placing one or more messages into transit with age zero), delivery (selectively delivering some in-transit messages to their intended receiver), and time-progress ticks that increase the age of all in-transit packets by one.

- Functional requirements:
  - Any message put into the channel is represented as a container carrying the message payload and a nonnegative integer age.
  - Sending can insert any finite set of valid messages into the channel at age zero.
  - Delivery may nondeterministically deliver any subset of in-transit containers whose payloads are addressed to the same receiver; delivered containers are removed from transit and their payloads are presented as the delivery set for that step.
  - Time-progress increments the age field of every container currently in transit by exactly one and does not deliver messages.

- Correctness properties to guarantee:
  - Type safety: the collection of containers and the delivered payloads always conform to their declared domains (containers have payload+age, delivered values are valid messages).
  - No spurious loss: a message is removed from transit only when it is delivered.
  - Message isolation by receiver: a delivery event only yields messages addressed to the same receiver.
  - Progress/absence-of-stuckness: time ticks and send actions remain enabled as long as there exist messages or potential sends; deliveries may nondeterministically occur but cannot produce payloads not present as in-transit containers.
  - Age monotonicity: for each individual container, its recorded age increases by one on each time tick and starts at zero when sent.

Also state which artifacts are considered atomic observations (the set of in-transit containers and the set of messages produced by a delivery event) and require that deliveries expose only message payloads (not ages).

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies an eventually perfect failure detector in a partially synchronous distributed system. Each process maintains a local clock, a suspicion set, timeout values for other processes, and counters for how long it has been since it last heard from them; processes periodically send "alive" messages, receive incoming messages supplied by the environment, and periodically predict failures based on timeout expiration. The specification models adaptive timeouts by increasing a timeout when a previously suspected process is heard from again, and it includes a type invariant but no full temporal specification such as Spec, fairness, or liveness properties.

This specification models Dijkstra's first published mutual exclusion algorithm, as described in his 1965 CACM paper. The algorithm ensures mutual exclusion among a set of processes (Proc), each of which cycles through non-critical and critical sections, using shared variables b, c, and k. The PlusCal translation is provided, and the TLA+ translation defines the system's state, actions, and temporal properties. The model checks mutual exclusion, deadlock freedom (under weak fairness), and discusses starvation freedom, with explicit invariants and liveness properties. The design allows for arbitrary process names and includes detailed commentary on the translation and fairness requirements.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal TLA+ model of Dijkstra’s original mutual‑exclusion algorithm for an arbitrary finite set of concurrent processes. The model should describe processes that repeatedly attempt to enter a critical section, execute it, and then return to a non‑critical remainder. Each process may read and write shared Boolean flags and a shared selector variable used to suggest which process should next be favored.

The specification must capture the intended behavior (not an implementation): processes may loop trying to enter the critical section, can examine other processes’ published state in arbitrary order, and may update the shared selector to influence contention. Processes must be allowed to make nondeterministic choices about the order in which they check others. The model should not assume fairness beyond what is explicitly required for particular liveness properties.

Require and prove these correctness properties:

- Mutual exclusion: no two distinct processes are ever simultaneously in their critical sections.
- Deadlock freedom (weak form): whenever some process is trying to enter the critical section, eventually some process (not necessarily the same one) will enter a critical section, under the usual fairness assumption that a continuously enabled process action is not perpetually ignored.
- Deadlock freedom (strong form): whenever any process is in the trying region (i.e., not in the final non‑critical state), eventually some process will enter the critical section, taking into account that processes may legitimately remain forever in the non‑critical remainder.
- Starvation characterization: specify the property of starvation freedom (each trying process eventually enters), and show whether the algorithm satisfies or violates it.

Also specify initial conditions (all flags in the initial state set to indicate non‑interest) and allow parameterization by the set of processes. Include invariants and temporal properties suitable for model checking with TLC and for proving with TLA+.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models Dijkstra's first published mutual exclusion algorithm for an arbitrary set of processes Proc, using a PlusCal algorithm and its generated TLA+ translation. The system uses shared variables b, c, and k together with per-process control state pc and a temporary local variable temp to represent each process progressing through entry protocol, critical section, and non-critical section. The specification includes the initial condition, next-state relation, and a fairness-based temporal specification Spec, and it defines safety and liveness properties including MutualExclusion, DeadlockFree, StarvationFree, and a stronger DeadlockFreedom property under an alternative liveness specification LSpec.
desc_intent:
Model Dijkstra’s original mutual-exclusion algorithm for N concurrently executing processes (an arbitrary finite set). The model should describe the behavior of each process as it repeatedly attempts to enter a critical section, executes it, then performs noncritical work before trying again. The model must capture the shared state used by the algorithm (simple Boolean flags per process and a single shared pointer used for arbitration) and allow nondeterministic scheduling of processes and nondeterministic examination order of other processes when checking flags. Do not prescribe a particular implementation style; instead specify the abstract operations each process performs: announce intent, inspect and update the shared pointer under the algorithm’s rules, scan other processes’ announcements in some arbitrary order, enter and leave the critical section, and reset its announcement. Require fairness assumptions sufficient to rule out unjustified perpetual starvation of enabled steps but allow a process to remain forever in the noncritical section unless specified otherwise.

Specify the following correctness properties to be checked:
- Safety (mutual exclusion): at most one process may be in the critical section at any time.
- Liveness (deadlock freedom): if some process is trying to enter the critical section (is beyond the initial noncritical step), then eventually some process will enter the critical section (under appropriate fairness).
- Optional liveness (starvation freedom): if desired, state the stronger property that each process that tries indefinitely eventually enters its critical section, and note that the model should allow demonstrating whether this stronger property holds or can be violated.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies Dijkstra's first published mutual exclusion algorithm, presented as a PlusCal algorithm together with its generated TLA+ translation. It models an arbitrary set Proc of processes that compete to enter a critical section using shared boolean arrays b and c and a shared process-valued variable k, with weak fairness assumptions for process steps in the main specification. The file defines the initial condition, per-control-location actions, the overall next-state relation and specification, and then states safety and liveness properties including mutual exclusion, deadlock freedom, starvation freedom, and a stronger deadlock-freedom property under a modified fairness interpretation.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal TLA+ model of a distributed mutual-exclusion algorithm in which an arbitrary finite set of concurrent processes repeatedly attempt to enter a single critical section. The model should capture the protocol’s coordination state and any per-process flags or tokens used to indicate intent to enter or release the critical section, plus a shared selector or pointer that one process may change to influence which process is favored next. Processes repeatedly perform a noncritical phase, a protocol to acquire permission, a critical section, and a release phase that restores their flags and the selector appropriately. Model nondeterministic scheduling and nondeterministic choices of the order in which a process inspects other processes’ flags.

Require the following correctness properties:
- Safety (mutual exclusion): at most one process may be in the critical section at any time.
- Deadlock-freedom under weak fairness: if some process is trying to enter the critical section (i.e., it is in the entry protocol), then eventually some process (not necessarily the same one) will enter the critical section, assuming processes that can take steps are not permanently disabled.
- Distinguish starvation: do not require starvation-freedom (it is acceptable that a particular waiting process might never enter), but allow the model to exhibit starvation counterexamples.
- Liveness nuance for nonblocking remainder: allow processes to remain forever in the noncritical section; when modeling fairness, ensure fairness obligations do not force progress for processes that choose to stay in their noncritical section.

Do not prescribe particular variable names or implementation structure; focus on the abstract actions and the temporal properties the model must satisfy.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a disk-based variant of Synod/Paxos in which processes interact through persistent disks and maintain local phase, block, and read/write bookkeeping state. The model assumes each process has a disjoint positive ballot set, a distinguished set of disks with a majority predicate, and requires that any two disk majorities intersect. The specification defines initialization, phase-0 recovery reads, phase-1 and phase-2 writes and reads, ballot restarts, and failures, then verifies that the overall behavior refinement-style implies the imported SynodSpec theorem target.
desc_intent:
Specify a distributed consensus protocol for a set of processes that use a set of durable storage nodes (disks) to achieve single-value agreement across potentially multiple ballots. The model should capture processes proposing values, attempting ballots, writing and reading value/ballot records to and from disks, and progressing through logical phases (prepare/accept-like phases and a read phase). The system must tolerate arbitrary interleavings and crashes or resets of processes (but not disk failures) and must allow processes to restart ballots later with higher ballot numbers.

Requirements:
- Processes may propose inputs and must be able to start a ballot with a ballot number from an allowed per-process ballot space; distinct processes have disjoint ballot-number sets.
- Processes perform two-phase interactions with disks: a phase that gathers disk state by reading majority responses, and a phase that writes chosen blocks to disks and then collects acknowledgements from a majority before committing.
- Disk blocks store a pair of ballot metadata and a proposed value (or a marker for no value). Reads return the whole block previously written at that disk for a specific process.
- A ballot must choose the value with highest seen ballot among read blocks if any non-empty values are observed; otherwise the proposer’s own input may be chosen.
- Processes must only accept (decide/commit) values after obtaining confirmation from a majority of disks.
- Process failures allow their local state to be reset and for other processes to proceed; disk contents persist across failures.
- Safety property: at most one value can ever be chosen (agreement) and any chosen value must equal some process’s input (validity).
- Liveness goal (optional): if a non-faulty process eventually runs with sufficiently high ballots and a majority of disks respond, then some value will be chosen.

Model should abstractly represent disks, majority predicate, per-process ballot domains, and the necessary invariants ensuring that majority-written state overlaps so safety holds. Do not prescribe a particular implementation; specify behavior and correctness properties.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module augments the DiskSynod specification with additional history variables and inductive invariants for a disk-based Synod/Paxos-style consensus protocol. It introduces `allInput` to track every input value ever seen and `chosen` to record the first non-default output produced by any process, then states a series of higher-level invariants relating ballots, disk blocks, reads, majority sets, and the chosen value. The file does not define a full temporal specification of its own, but instead builds on the imported `Init` and `Next` actions from `DiskSynod` and adds safety-oriented predicates that characterize correctness of the protocol state.
desc_intent:
Specify a TLA+ model of a replicated, disk-backed consensus protocol that ensures a single input value can become chosen by a majority of disks despite concurrent proposers and failures.
