Include fairness assumptions sufficient to prevent livelock (e.g., weak fairness for actions that enable progress). Express safety properties: values in the channel must be unchanged while buffered; acknowledgement occurs only for a previously offered value; and the channel buffer capacity constraint is respected. Express liveness properties: every value offered in the presence of a continuously eager receiver is eventually delivered and acknowledged; and if a participant repeatedly attempts to send or receive, progress will eventually occur under the fairness assumptions.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module defines a TLC-specific state constraint for model checking an instanced inner FIFO specification without modifying the underlying specification module. The comments explain that the underlying FIFO spec has an unbounded state space because the queue q can grow arbitrarily large, so this wrapper module introduces a constant bound qLen and a predicate qConstraint that restricts the queue length to be at most qLen. The file does not define the FIFO algorithm itself, any actions, or temporal properties; it only adds a finite-state constraint intended to be referenced from a TLC configuration.
desc_intent:
Model a parameterized inner FIFO queue used inside a concurrent system. The model should describe a single FIFO buffer that holds a sequence of messages (from a given finite message domain), supports enqueue and dequeue operations, and can be instantiated multiple times by clients. The queue must preserve message order (first-in, first-out), never lose or duplicate messages, and correctly handle empty-queue and full-queue conditions. The specification must allow an arbitrary but fixed maximum capacity chosen at instantiation time, and must make explicit which operations are enabled when the queue is full or empty.

Specify the behavioral interface: an enqueue request must either succeed (appending the message to the tail) when capacity permits, or be rejected/blocked when full; a dequeue request must either succeed (removing and returning the head message) when the queue is nonempty, or fail/return an “empty” indication when empty. Model concurrent clients issuing enqueues and dequeues nondeterministically. Include invariants guaranteeing that the sequence of delivered (dequeued) messages is a prefix of the sequence of enqueued messages and that each enqueued message is eventually either retained in the queue or dequeued (no silent loss). Include safety properties: preservation of FIFO ordering, capacity bound, and absence of duplicates. Optionally state liveness properties: progress under weak fairness (e.g., an enabled dequeue or enqueue will eventually execute).

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a thin wrapper around an existing hour-clock specification, providing Apalache type annotations while keeping the original specification separate. The comments explain that it applies annotations to HourClock2.tla via INSTANCE, and that HourClock2 is an alternative formulation of HourClock using `(hr % 12) + 1` instead of an `IF`-`THEN`-`ELSE`. The file itself declares the clock variable `hr`, extends Naturals, and instantiates the module `HourClock2`, but it contains no top-level behavioral operators, actions, or temporal properties of its own.
desc_intent:
Specify a simple 12-hour clock counter that models the behavior of an hours display which cycles through values 1..12. The model should represent the clock's state as the currently displayed hour and allow a single step action that advances the display by one hour. When advancing, the clock must increment the hour modulo 12 so that after 12 the next displayed value is 1. The model must allow any initial displayed hour to be any integer in the allowed range 1..12.

State the safety and liveness properties the system must guarantee:
- Safety: the displayed hour is always an integer in the range 1..12; no step can produce a value outside that range.
- Determinism of the step action: from any state there is exactly one enabled step that computes the next hour.
- Correct wraparound: taking one step from hour 12 yields 1, and for any hour h in 1..11 a step yields h+1.

Specify an invariant capturing the legal range and a step relation capturing the modulo-12 increment semantics. Also state a simple liveness property that every hour value will be reached infinitely often under repeated stepping (fairness / eventual reachability of each of the twelve hours).

desc_declarative_gpt: This module, APHourClock, provides Apalache type annotations for the HourClock specification by using INSTANCE to avoid modifying the original HourClock.tla file. It declares a single variable 'hr' and annotates it with the type Int using a comment. The module extends Naturals to provide natural number arithmetic, and it instantiates the HourClock module, presumably to inherit its definitions and structure. No operators, actions, or temporal properties are defined directly in this file; its purpose is to serve as a typed wrapper for model checking or analysis tools that require explicit type information.
desc_intent:
Specify a discrete, cyclic hour clock abstraction that counts hours modulo 12 and supports asynchronous external adjustments. The model should treat the clock value as an integer in 0..11 representing the current hour. The system must allow two kinds of events: normal ticks that advance the hour by one modulo 12, and external set operations that replace the current hour with any allowed value. Both event types can occur non-deterministically and may occur concurrently from the perspective of the environment, but the model should represent the clock as a single atomic update per event.

Require the following correctness properties:
- Safety: the clock value is always within the valid range 0..11.
- Progress: it is always possible for the clock to eventually change (i.e., ticks are not permanently disabled).
- Deterministic wrap-around: repeated ticks must cycle through the 12-hour sequence and return to the starting value after 12 successive ticks.
- Set consistency: when an external set operation writes a new hour, the resulting value must equal the written value immediately after the operation.
- No lost updates under serial execution: if two update events occur sequentially, the final value reflects the second event (the model need not enforce concurrency control beyond atomic events).

Also state invariants and temporal properties needed to assert the above, and expose the initial condition where the clock starts at some value in 0..11 (not fixed).

desc_declarative_gpt: This module defines an alternative hour-clock specification named HC2 for the clock model introduced in the extended module HourClock. It introduces a next-state action HCnxt2 that advances the hour by setting hr' to (hr % 12) + 1, and defines HC2 as the conjunction of the inherited initial condition HCini with the temporal formula [][HCnxt2]_hr. The module also states a theorem asserting that the inherited specification HC is equivalent to HC2, showing that the alternative next-state formulation yields the same behavior.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module `HourClock2` is an extension of the `HourClock` module that defines an alternative but equivalent formulation of a 12-hour clock specification. It inherits the variable `hr`, the initial condition `HCini` (constraining `hr` to be in the range 1–12), and the arithmetic operators from the base module.

The module introduces `HCnxt2`, an alternative next-state relation defined as `hr' = (hr % 12) + 1`, which advances the hour by computing the modulus before adding one. This contrasts with the original `HCnxt` from `HourClock`, though both produce the same cyclic 1-through-12 behavior. The full specification `HC2` is formed as `HCini /\ [][HCnxt2]_hr`, a standard TLA+ safety specification with stuttering-tolerant next-state steps. The module also states the theorem that `HC` and `HC2` are logically equivalent, asserting that the two formulations describe exactly the same set of behaviors.

The accompanying model-checking configuration uses `HC` as the specification and checks `HC2` as a property, directing TLC to verify that every behavior satisfying `HC` also satisfies `HC2`. This serves as a model-checking test of the equivalence theorem in one direction.
desc_intent: Write a TLA+ specification that demonstrates the equivalence of two formulations of a 12-hour clock. The clock has a single variable representing the current hour, which ranges from 1 to 12. The initial condition sets the hour to some value in that range, and each step advances the hour forward by one, wrapping from 12 back to 1. The primary formulation expresses the next-state transition by checking whether the hour equals 12 and resetting to 1, or otherwise incrementing by 1. A second equivalent formulation expresses the same transition more compactly using modular arithmetic. The specification should extend an existing HourClock module and define the alternative next-state relation and the combined specification built from the shared initial condition. The key correctness property to verify is that the two specifications — the base one and the modular-arithmetic variant — are equivalent, meaning each implies the other. The module should include a theorem asserting this equivalence, and the model checker configuration should verify that the primary specification satisfies the alternative formulation as a temporal property.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a simple 12-hour clock. The state variable 'hr' represents the current hour, which ranges from 1 to 12. The initial predicate HCini ensures that the hour starts within this range. The next-state action HCnxt increments the hour by 1 unless it is 12, in which case it wraps around to 1. The temporal property HC asserts that the system starts in a valid hour and always takes valid next steps. The theorem proves that the invariant HCini is always maintained.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module models a simple 12-hour clock. The single variable `hr` represents the current hour. The initial condition `HCini` constrains `hr` to be a natural number in the range 1 through 12. The next-state relation `HCnxt` advances the clock by one hour each step, wrapping from 12 back to 1. The full specification `HC` combines the initial condition with a stuttering-tolerant always-`HCnxt` box action, allowing steps where `hr` remains unchanged alongside the normal tick transitions.

The module includes a theorem asserting that `HC` implies `[]HCini`, meaning the hour always remains within 1..12 throughout every execution. The accompanying TLC configuration file designates `HC` as the specification to check and `HCini` as an invariant, directing the model checker to verify that the hour variable never leaves the valid range. This is a small illustrative example demonstrating the basic structure of a TLA+ specification and the relationship between an initial predicate, a next-state action, and an always-satisfied safety invariant.
desc_intent: Write a TLA+ specification for a simple 12-hour clock. The clock maintains a single hour counter that always holds a value between 1 and 12 inclusive. Each tick of the clock advances the hour by one, wrapping from 12 back to 1. The system begins in any valid hour state and transitions by this cyclic increment rule, with stuttering steps permitted. The key correctness property to verify is that the hour value remains within the range 1 through 12 at all times — that is, the valid-hour condition is an invariant of the specification. The theorem to establish is that the overall clock specification implies this invariant holds forever. Configure the model checker to treat the clock formula as the specification under check and to verify the valid-hour range condition as an invariant.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module, APHourClock, provides Apalache type annotations for the Liveness/HourClock.tla specification. It is an exact duplicate of SpecifyingSystems/HourClock/HourClock.tla, but is kept separate so that other modules (such as those in the Specifying-Systems chapter on Liveness) can EXTEND HourClock from a sibling module. The module introduces a single variable 'hr' with an Apalache type annotation indicating it is an integer. No operators, actions, or temporal properties are defined directly in this file; instead, the module relies on the imported HourClock module for its behavior and properties.
desc_intent:
Specify a simple digital hour clock that maintains an integer hour value in the range 0..23 and advances time in discrete steps. The model should represent the state of the clock and a nondeterministic step that increments the hour by one modulo 24. Include an initialization that sets the hour to some valid integer in 0..23. The specification must allow repeated advancement steps forever.

State the obligations the model must verify:
- Safety: the hour is always an integer in 0..23.
- Determinacy of the wrap-around behavior: whenever the clock advances from 23, the next hour must be 0; for any other hour h in 0..22 the next hour must be h+1.
- Stuttering tolerance: allowing steps that do not change the hour (stuttering) is permitted, but such steps cannot violate safety or the wrap-around property.

Also require liveness properties:
- Progress: from any reachable state, the system must inevitably reach every hour value (i.e., each hour recurs infinitely often).
- Fairness: the advance step should not be indefinitely postponed (strong fairness ensuring eventual advancement whenever enabled).

Do not prescribe particular variable names or implementation structure; describe only the abstract state, transitions, invariants, and liveness requirements to be proved.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module, APLiveHourClock, serves as a type-annotated wrapper for the LiveHourClock specification. Its primary purpose is to provide Apalache type annotations for the variable 'hr' by declaring it with an explicit type comment. The module does not define any operators or properties itself, but instead instantiates the LiveHourClock module, substituting its own 'hr' variable for the one in LiveHourClock. No temporal properties, actions, or proofs are present; the design is focused on maintaining the original specification's clarity while enabling tool-specific type checking.
desc_intent: Specify a model of a simple hour clock that continuously tracks the current hour of a 12-hour dial and supports atomic adjustments. The system must maintain a single integer state representing the displayed hour, constrained to the values 1..12. It must provide two kinds of externally visible atomic transitions: an automatic tick that advances the hour by one (wrapping from 12 back to 1), and an explicit set operation that assigns the clock to any valid hour value. Both transitions may occur nondeterministically and repeatedly; time should be modeled as discrete steps of these transitions. The model must forbid invalid hour values and ensure the display always remains within the valid range. Key correctness properties to assert: (1) Invariance: the hour is always between 1 and 12 inclusive. (2) Progress: from any reachable state, it is possible to eventually reach any target hour value via some finite sequence of transitions (the system is strongly connected over the 12-hour states). (3) Wrap-around correctness: a tick when at hour 12 yields hour 1. Additionally, the model should allow specifying an initial hour nondeterministically among valid values and expose the tick and set actions for temporal reasoning and model checking.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module augments the hour clock specification from HourClock with a liveness requirement. It defines a specification LSpec that conjoins the inherited clock specification HC with a weak fairness condition WF_hr(HCnxt), ensuring the clock step HCnxt continues to occur fairly on the variable hr. The module also defines temporal properties stating that ticking happens infinitely often, every hour value from 1 through 12 recurs infinitely often, and the initial-state typing condition remains always true; it includes a theorem asserting these properties from LSpec and a postcondition describing a concrete counterexample structure for a settling property.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module extends the `HourClock` module to add liveness guarantees to the basic hour-clock specification. The underlying system, inherited from `HourClock`, models a 12-hour clock with a single variable `hr` ranging over 1..12, advancing by one hour on each tick and wrapping from 12 back to 1.

The module defines `LSpec` as the conjunction of the base `HC` specification and a weak-fairness condition `WF_hr(HCnxt)`, which ensures the clock tick action `HCnxt` is not indefinitely postponed. Three temporal properties are then stated and claimed to follow from `LSpec` via a `THEOREM`. `AlwaysTick` asserts that the clock ticks infinitely often, expressed as `[]<><<HCnxt>>_hr`. `AllTimes` asserts that every hour value from 1 to 12 is visited infinitely often, i.e., `\A n \in 1..12 : []<>(hr = n)`. `TypeInvariance` asserts that the type invariant `HCini` — which constrains `hr` to the domain 1..12 — holds in every reachable state, expressed as the temporal formula `[]HCini`. The TLC configuration file directs the model checker to verify all three properties against `LSpec`.
desc_intent: Write a TLA+ specification for a simple 12-hour clock that ticks forward continuously. The clock has a single variable representing the current hour, which ranges over 1 through 12. Each tick advances the hour by one, wrapping from 12 back to 1. The specification must include a fairness condition ensuring that the clock never stops ticking. Three properties must hold: first, ticking actions occur infinitely often; second, every hour value from 1 to 12 is visited infinitely often; and third, the hour variable always remains within the valid range 1 through 12. This module should extend a base hour-clock module that defines the state predicate and next-state relation, adding weak fairness on the tick action to produce the live specification, then state and verify the theorem that the live specification implies all three properties.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a TLC support module for model checking the specification of LiveInternalMemory. It provides concrete replacements for the constant operators Send, Reply, and InitMemInt so that TLC can evaluate transitions involving the internal memory interface, and it also defines a liveness formula requiring every processor to be busy infinitely often. In addition, it defines a large PostCondition value describing a specific counterexample trace as a structured record containing action and state snapshots.
desc_intent:
Specify a distributed shared-memory cache-coherence service that models an internal memory component interacting with processors and a coherence manager. The model should describe how processors issue memory requests (reads and writes) and how the internal memory accepts messages ("send" and "reply") that update its local state. The system must allow asynchronous message delivery from processors to the internal memory and from the internal memory back to processors, and must permit the internal memory state to be atomically replaced by a new value when it processes a message.

Require the model to capture the following behavior and correctness properties:

- The internal memory holds a value per processor interaction that can be updated only via well-formed request or reply messages; each update must explicitly replace the previous stored value with the new message payload.
- Initial state: the internal memory starts with a single, well-defined default entry representing "no value" associated with some processor.
- Safety: every state transition that models handling a send or reply must deterministically set the new internal-memory contents to the payload associated with that processing step; there must be no implicit nondeterministic modification of other internal-memory entries.
- Liveness: if a processor repeatedly issues a request, the model must allow eventual processing that updates the internal memory (no permanent starvation).
- Interaction constraints: messages carry the identifier of the originating processor and a data value; the internal memory must reflect those identifiers in its updates so observers can attribute updates to the correct sender.

Do not commit to implementation details such as variable names, encoding of messages, or a particular step-by-step algorithm; specify only the abstract state, atomic update semantics for handling messages, initial condition, and the safety and liveness requirements above.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a TLC model-checking wrapper for the write-through cache specification from LiveWriteThroughCache. It manually instantiates definitions corresponding to the internal-memory liveness specification, using a refinement mapping from the cache implementation state variables to abstract memory variables omem, octl, and obuf, because the comments explain that the TLC version targeted here cannot handle the intended INSTANCE-based instantiation directly. The file defines initial-state, next-state, type-invariant, enabledness, liveness, and combined specification formulas for the instantiated internal memory view, and also includes constants and a PostCondition value describing a counterexample-shaped structure for model checking.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal TLA+ model of a write-through cache controller that mediates requests from a fixed set of processors to a single coherent memory, and prove that it implements the externally visible behaviors of an abstract live memory interface under a refinement mapping.

Model the system as follows:
- There is a finite set of addresses and values, and a fixed set of processors issuing memory requests. Each processor may issue read or write requests.
- The cache controller exposes an external protocol to processors with the visible processor states: ready to issue a request, waiting for the controller to complete the request, and completed (ready again). Processors interact only via this protocol.
- The controller forwards requests immediately to the underlying memory (write-through): on a write request the memory is updated synchronously with the controller accepting the operation; on a read, the controller returns the current memory value for the requested address.
- The controller keeps, per-processor, a small per-request buffer recording the outstanding request or the returned value or a no-value marker.
- Internal communication between controller and memory is abstracted as an internal message or internal state used only to model interaction, not visible to processors.

Require the specification to guarantee:
- Safety: every read returns the most recently written value for that address (linearizability/refinement to the abstract memory mapping of addresses to values). External traces of processor-visible state and returned values must correspond to some legal sequence of operations on an abstract memory.
- Progress/liveness: if a processor is waiting to perform an operation, then eventually either the controller performs the operation (updates memory and produces a reply) or the situation that enables the operation disappears; formally capture fair execution of enabled internal Do/Reply transitions so that enabled requests cannot be permanently ignored.
- Determinacy of visible control states: the controller never leaves a processor permanently in a busy state without eventually moving it to done and then ready, under the fairness assumptions.

Do not commit to a particular implementation structure; instead state the observable variables (processor-visible control states, per-processor buffers holding requests/results, and the abstract memory mapping) and require that the implementation refine the abstract live memory interface via a mapping from internal state to the abstract memory and processor-visible control/buffer values.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a small TLA+ example that uses ASSUME statements to have TLC check the truth of simple mathematical and logical formulas. It models no stateful algorithm and introduces no variables; instead, it evaluates propositional logic and elementary set-theoretic identities over constants a through g, booleans, and finite sets. The file demonstrates bounded quantification, logical equivalences, and basic set operators, and defines a helper operator SomeSets as the powerset of {a, b, c, d, e}.
desc_intent: Specify a formal model of a small, static mathematics-checking environment that can validate basic logical and set-theoretic identities over a finite domain of values. The model should expose a finite collection of named, distinct constant values and allow expressions built from Boolean values, natural numbers, and those constants. It must permit checking of propositional identities (e.g., implications, disjunction, conjunction, negation) over the two-valued Boolean domain, verifying tautologies and non-tautologies. It must allow construction and comparison of finite sets and multisets composed of the constants and numbers, supporting equality, subset, union, intersection, set difference, membership, and powerset. The model should be able to assert universally quantified properties over bounded domains (finite sets of booleans or explicitly enumerated subsets) and report whether each asserted formula holds. Key correctness properties: every asserted tautology over the Boolean domain must be provably true in the model; assertions that are not logical tautologies must be detectable as false for some assignment in the bounded domain; set operations must obey standard set-theoretic laws (e.g., idempotence and equality of sets ignoring multiplicity, subset relationships, and that the powerset operator yields exactly all subsets of the base set). The specification should avoid modeling unbounded quantification or choice and limit its universe to finite, explicitly enumerated values.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies the correctness skeleton of the alternating-bit protocol using sender and receiver bit variables together with sent and received data values. The sender may send a new value when its acknowledgement bit matches its send bit, the receiver may accept a message when its receive bit differs from the sender bit, and the sender may accept an acknowledgement when the receiver bit differs from the sender acknowledgement bit. The specification defines an initial condition, a next-state relation, a type invariant, fairness assumptions for message reception and acknowledgement reception, and a temporal property stating that the sender and acknowledgement bits are infinitely often out of sync.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module ABCorrectness specifies an idealized, channel-free reference model of the Alternating Bit Protocol, intended to capture the correct high-level behavior against which a full implementation can be verified (e.g., via refinement mapping).

The state consists of a sender bit `sBit`, a sender acknowledgement `sAck`, a receiver bit `rBit`, a currently-sent data value `sent`, and a most-recently received data value `rcvd`, all over a finite set `Data` (instantiated as `{d1, d2}`). Initialization allows any consistent starting state where all three bits agree. The action `CSndNewValue` fires when the sender has been acknowledged (`sAck = sBit`), picks a new data value, and flips `sBit` to signal a new transmission. `CRcvMsg` fires when the receiver's bit differs from the sender's, updating `rBit` and copying `sent` into `rcvd` to model successful message delivery. `CRcvAck` fires when the sender's acknowledgement lags behind the receiver's bit, advancing `sAck` to match `rBit`. Weak fairness is required on both `CRcvMsg` and `CRcvAck`, ensuring that pending deliveries and acknowledgements are eventually processed. The specification `ABCSpec` combines initialization, the stuttering-closed next-state relation, and the fairness conditions. The only checked property is the type invariant `TypeInv`, which asserts all bits remain in `{0,1}` and data values stay within `Data`.
desc_intent: Write a TLA+ specification for an abstract correctness model of the Alternating Bit Protocol. The system involves a sender and receiver exchanging data values, tracked through control bits and acknowledgment bits rather than explicit message channels. The sender holds a current data value and a send bit; when its acknowledgment bit matches its send bit, it may choose a new data value and toggle the send bit to indicate a pending transmission. The receiver copies the sent value and flips its own bit to match the sender's bit when it detects a discrepancy. The sender advances its acknowledgment bit to track the receiver's bit, again when they differ. The specification should maintain a type invariant asserting all bits are boolean (0 or 1) and both data variables are drawn from the given Data constant. Liveness is enforced by requiring that the receive and acknowledge actions are weakly fair, ensuring that if the receiver can copy a message or the sender can update its acknowledgment, these actions will eventually occur. The overall specification combines the initial condition, the stuttering-tolerant next-state relation, and these fairness conditions.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a model-checking harness around an alternating-bit protocol specification imported from another module. It adds queue-length constraints, states liveness and temporal properties about sent data eventually being received and about possible permanent disagreement of protocol bits, and records a concrete postcondition/counterexample structure using TLC-style trace data. The file also introduces a derived action-temporal formula and a simple stability property over sent data, while composing a combined specification from the imported protocol specification and an added temporal condition.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal TLA+ model of the alternating bit protocol for reliable delivery over unreliable channels. The model should represent two endpoints, a sender and a receiver, exchanging data messages and acknowledgements over lossy, possibly reordering channels with bounded queue capacity. The sender repeatedly transmits items from an unbounded stream of application data, attaching a one-bit sequence number; the receiver accepts in-order data only and returns acknowledgements carrying the bit of the last correctly received packet. If a message or acknowledgement is lost or delayed, the sender will retransmit until it receives the expected acknowledgement matching the current bit; the receiver must discard duplicate deliveries. The environment may arbitrarily drop or reorder messages but must preserve message contents.

Specify safety properties:
- No spurious application deliveries: the receiver must deliver only items actually sent by the sender.
- In-order delivery modulo duplicates: delivered application items must appear in the same order they were originally sent.
- Sequence correctness: acknowledgements and data are only accepted when their sequence bit matches the protocol expectations; duplicates are detected and not redelivered.

Specify liveness properties:
- Eventual delivery under fair retransmission: for every sent data item, if the sender continues to retransmit under weak fairness of its send action, then the item is eventually delivered to the receiver.
- Progress fairness: if messages are continuously enabled to be sent and the network does not permanently drop all copies, then acknowledgements eventually arrive enabling sender progress.

Require parameters for channel capacities and the data domain. Do not prescribe an implementation strategy; instead describe the abstract actions, allowed failures, and the correctness invariants and temporal guarantees the specification must enforce.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module models the classic balance-scale stone-cutting problem: given a total weight W and N pieces, find an ordered partition of W into N natural-number weights such that every target weight from 1 to W can be balanced using those pieces on either side of the scale. The specification encodes weighing by allowing coefficients in {-1, 0, 1}, where a negative coefficient represents placing a piece on the same side as the object being weighed. It uses recursive operators to enumerate ordered partitions and to sum sequences, and then uses TLC-oriented ASSUME formulas with PrintT to search for and display a solution or report that no solution exists.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module encodes and solves the Car Talk balance-scale puzzle: given a stone of weight W pounds and a balance scale, find N pieces whose weights allow any integer weight from 1 to W to be measured. Because pieces may be placed on either side of the scale, each piece contributes a coefficient of −1, 0, or +1, so the problem reduces to finding a sequence of N positive integers summing to W such that every integer in 1..W can be expressed as a signed combination of those integers.

The module defines two key operators. `Partitions(seq, wt)` recursively enumerates all non-decreasing sequences of N natural numbers that sum to W, pruning the search using tight bounds on valid element ranges. `Weighs(seq, wt)` checks whether a given partition can represent a target weight by existentially quantifying over coefficient assignments from {−1, 0, 1} applied to each piece. The central `ASSUME` statement directs TLC to search all such ordered partitions and, for each one, test whether every weight in 1..W is achievable; if a valid partition is found, it is printed via `PrintT`; otherwise the string "No solution" is printed. The module has no variables, no state transitions, and no temporal properties — it is purely a model-checking computation wrapper that exploits TLC's assumption-evaluation mechanism to solve a combinatorial puzzle, with the default configuration setting W = 40 and N = 4.
desc_intent: Write a TLA+ specification that solves the following puzzle: given a balance scale and a single stone of weight W pounds, cut it into exactly N pieces such that any integer weight from 1 to W pounds can be measured. Because pieces may be placed on either side of the balance, each piece effectively contributes a positive, negative, or zero amount to the measured weight. The task is to find an ordered partition of W into N positive integer parts such that every integer weight between 1 and W can be expressed as a signed sum of those parts, where each coefficient is drawn from {-1, 0, 1}. The specification should enumerate candidate partitions efficiently by considering only non-decreasing sequences of positive integers summing to W, and use TLC to evaluate an assumption that either prints a valid partition when one exists or prints "No solution" otherwise. W and N should be provided as constants, with the motivating case being W = 40 and N = 4.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies an N-process shared-memory algorithm in which each process writes its own shared register and then reads a neighbor's register, using regular registers rather than atomic registers for the shared x values. The model represents a regular register by a set of possible values, so a write from 0 to 1 is modeled by first changing a register value from {0} to {0,1} and then to {1}; a read may return any element currently in that set. The specification defines the translated PlusCal actions, an initial condition, the next-state relation, a termination condition, a safety property PCorrect stating that if all processes are done then some y[i] equals 1, an inductive invariant Inv used to prove that property, and two TLAPS proofs establishing correctness.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies an N-process shared-memory algorithm that is a variant of a simpler algorithm (from module Simple), modified to use *regular registers* instead of atomic registers. Each process `i` in the range `0..N-1` has a shared register `x[i]`, modeled as a non-empty subset of `{0,1}` to capture the semantics of a regular register, and a local register `y[i]` holding a value in `{0,1}`.

Each process executes three steps: at `a1` it sets `x[self]` to `{0,1}` (representing the transient state during a write of 1 over the old value 0); at `a2` it completes the write by setting `x[self]` to `{1}`; at `b` it reads a nondeterministically chosen value from `x[(self-1) % N]` into `y[self]`, modeling that a regular-register read may return any value currently in the register's value set. The specification `Spec` is the initial condition plus a stuttering-closed next-state relation, with a `Termination` liveness property asserting all processes eventually reach `Done`.

The safety property `PCorrect` asserts that when all processes have finished, at least one process read the value 1. The inductive invariant `Inv` combines a type invariant `TypeOK` with two structural conditions: every process at or past label `b` has already completed its write (`x[i] = {1}`), and either some process is not yet done or some `y[i]` equals 1. Two TLAPS-verified theorems, `Correctness` and `Correctness2`, prove that `Spec` implies `[]PCorrect` using this inductive invariant. The model-checking configuration sets `N = 8` and checks `PCorrect`, `TypeOK`, and `Inv` as invariants.
desc_intent:
Specify an N-process shared-memory algorithm in which each process i owns a shared register and a private local register. Each process performs three steps: it begins writing the value 1 to its shared register (entering a transitional state where the register may return either its old value 0 or the new value 1), completes the write so the register stably holds 1, and then reads the shared register of its left neighbor (process (i−1) mod N) into its local register. The shared registers are regular rather than atomic: during an ongoing write from old value to new value, a concurrent read may nondeterministically return either the old or the new value, and this must be modeled explicitly.

The key correctness property is that when all N processes have finished, at least one process must have read the value 1 into its local register. The specification must prove this safety property as an invariant. Additionally, the system must be live in that all processes eventually complete. The specification should be verified for concrete values of N (e.g., N = 8) and include a proof of the safety property using an inductive invariant.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a simple concurrent ring algorithm with N processes arranged in a circle. Each process first sets its own x entry to 1, then copies the left neighbor's x value into its own y entry; the specification includes the PlusCal algorithm in comments and its translated TLA+ form with variables x, y, and pc. The model assumes N is a positive natural number, defines the behavior with Init, Next, and Spec, asserts termination as eventual completion of all processes, and proves a safety property stating that when all processes are done, at least one process has y[i] = 1. The file also develops an inductive invariant Inv, includes type correctness constraints, and contains TLAPS proofs of the main correctness theorem in two versions.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies a simple concurrent algorithm in which N processes, numbered 0 through N−1 and conceptually arranged in a circle, each execute two sequential steps. In step `a`, process `i` writes 1 into shared array `x` at index `i`. In step `b`, it reads `x` at the left-neighbor index `(i−1) mod N` and writes that value into shared array `y` at index `i`. All processes begin at label `a`, and the PlusCal translation produces variables `x`, `y` (both initialized to all-zeros arrays over {0,1}), and a program-counter array `pc` tracking each process's current label among `{"a", "b", "Done"}`. The constant `N` is assumed to be a positive natural number; the model-checking configuration fixes it to 5.

The core correctness property, `PCorrect`, asserts that when all processes have terminated, at least one process `i` has `y[i] = 1`. The module proves `Spec => []PCorrect` using TLAPS by establishing an inductive invariant `Inv`, which combines type-correctness (`TypeOK`) with two additional conjuncts: that any process past label `a` has already set `x[i] = 1`, and that either some process has not yet finished or some `y[i]` is already 1. Two TLAPS theorems (`Correctness` and `Correctness2`) formally verify this invariance, the latter being a more concise proof accepted by the same proof system. TLC is also configured to check `PCorrect`, `TypeOK`, and `Inv` as invariants against the specification.
desc_intent: Write a TLA+ specification for a simple concurrent algorithm in which N processes, numbered 0 through N−1 and arranged conceptually in a circle, each perform two sequential steps. In the first step a process writes 1 to its own slot in a shared array. In the second step it reads its left neighbor's slot (using modular indexing) and stores that value in a second shared array. Both arrays are initialized to all zeros. The key correctness property to verify is that once every process has finished, at least one entry in the second array equals 1. This postcondition must be proved as a safety invariant: it must hold in every reachable state where all processes have terminated. The specification should also establish that all processes eventually terminate. Provide a suitable inductive invariant that implies the postcondition and can be verified by a theorem prover such as TLAPS, capturing both type correctness and the structural reason the postcondition holds.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module defines several equivalent TLA+ formulations of the transitive closure of a binary relation represented as a set of ordered pairs. It develops multiple definitions: one based on paths as sequences, one using bounded sequences for finite relations, one using iterative relational composition, one recursive closure formulation, one Warshall-style recursive algorithm, and one formulation for relations represented as Boolean-valued operators over a set. The module uses assumptions to check, on small finite instances, that these different definitions are equivalent; it does not model a concurrent system or fault model, but rather specifies and compares mathematical definitions and their TLC-evaluable variants.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal model of the transitive closure of a binary relation and prove key equivalences between different characterizations. The model should treat a relation as a set of ordered pairs over some carrier and must be able to express the following notions and guarantees without prescribing a particular implementation:

- Define the support of a relation (the set of elements that appear in some pair) and treat the transitive closure as a relation on that support.
- Provide multiple independent characterizations of transitive closure and state their intended equivalence:
  - A path-based characterization: two elements are related iff there exists a finite nontrivial path of edges connecting them.
  - An iterative bounded-path characterization suitable for finite supports: existence of a connecting path whose length is bounded by the size of the support.
  - An algebraic closure via repeated relation composition and union: the union of R, R∘R, R∘R∘R, ... up to the support size.
  - A recursive doubling/closure method that repeatedly composes the relation with itself until saturation.
  - A node-elimination (Warshall-like) characterization that incrementally permits intermediate vertices.
- Require correctness properties:
  - Each characterization must yield a relation that is transitive and contains the original relation.
  - For finite relations, all characterizations must be provably equal to one another and equal to the minimal transitive superset (the standard transitive closure).
  - The support of the closure must equal the support of the original relation.
- Allow an alternate representation where relations are Boolean-valued predicates on pairs; provide a corresponding iterative construction and prove it matches the set-based definitions on finite supports.

Do not prescribe algorithmic steps; specify only the mathematical properties, invariants, and equivalence theorems that the model must establish.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a very small wrapper around another specification, declaring three variables p, c, and x, defining two simple helper operators, and instantiating the module TwoPhase. The operator XInit specifies an initial-state condition requiring its argument to equal 0, and XAct specifies a trivial next-state relation equating xNext with xInit. The file itself contains no temporal specification, no explicit safety or liveness theorem, and no fault model; it appears to provide parameterized initialization and action helpers for use with the instantiated module.
desc_intent:
Specify a two-phase protocol for a single shared register updated by a producer and read by a consumer. The system has a producer that prepares and commits updates in two logical phases and a consumer that may read the register at any time. Model the register's initial value and the producer’s two-phase update behavior (prepare then commit) as abstract state transitions, without prescribing a particular coding structure. The protocol must ensure atomic visibility of committed updates: a consumer must never observe a partially prepared update. Allow the consumer to read concurrently with producer actions and permit the producer to retry or reprepare before committing. Capture nondeterministic scheduling and asynchronous steps of both parties.

Specify safety properties: (1) reads return either the initial value or some fully committed value produced by the producer; (2) the prepare phase must not make new values visible until a matching commit occurs; (3) once a value is committed it remains visible to subsequent reads unless overwritten by a later commit. Also specify liveness expectations: eventual progress of committed updates under fair scheduling (if the producer continuously attempts to commit, some commit should eventually occur), and absence of indefinite blocking of the consumer. Provide invariants and temporal properties that formalize these safety and liveness requirements.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a model-checking wrapper around an instantiated YoYoNoPruning specification, using a fixed graph of nodes and edges and exposing a liveness-style postcondition over the imported state variables phase, incoming, outgoing, and mailbox. It defines a small graph directly in the module, includes a larger alternative graph in comments, and instantiates the YoYoNoPruning module without substitutions. The file does not define the algorithm's transition relation itself; instead, it records a temporal property stating that eventually all nodes remain permanently in the "down" phase, and it embeds a TLC-generated counterexample object as PostCondition showing a violating behavior trace and reachable states.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal model of a distributed graph algorithm in which a fixed set of processes occupy the vertices of an undirected graph and communicate only with neighbors. The system must support asynchronous message passing with reliable delivery but arbitrary delays. Each process should execute local computation and send messages along incident edges; it may buffer messages in per-process mailboxes. The goal is to elect and/or recognize a structural property of the graph (for example, to build a spanning forest, propagate information from sources, or compute neighborhood-based decisions) using a phase-based synchronous concept simulated over the asynchronous network: processes proceed through logical phases, exchange inbound and outbound information with neighbors, and update state accordingly.

Model the progression through phases, the sending and receiving of messages, and the constraints on message content and delivery without prescribing a particular implementation technique. Specify invariants that must always hold (e.g., message contents remain consistent with sender state, no message duplication beyond reliable delivery, and mailboxes contain only messages from neighbors). Define safety properties: local states and edge states must never contradict (for instance, a process cannot claim to have accepted a neighbor's proposal without receiving the corresponding message), and the system must avoid deadlocks where all processes wait indefinitely without progress. Specify liveness properties: every message sent is eventually delivered, and the protocol must make progress across phases (e.g., after finitely many steps all correct processes advance beyond any given phase, and a global stable configuration satisfying the intended graph-level outcome is eventually reached). Include the ability to reason about arbitrary finite graphs, arbitrary initial states, and the potential for concurrent message exchanges.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a model-checking wrapper for a Yo-Yo pruning specification. It defines a fixed graph using the operator definitions Nodes and Edges, declares the state variables active, phase, incoming, outgoing, and mailbox, and instantiates the module YoYoPruning. The file itself contains no transition relation, initialization predicate, temporal specification, assumptions, or proof content.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal model of a distributed graph pruning protocol that removes redundant vertices while preserving connectivity of a spanning subgraph. The system consists of a fixed undirected graph of processors (nodes) connected by edges. Each processor holds local state and can send/receive messages along incident edges. The protocol proceeds in asynchronous rounds/phases where processors decide locally whether to deactivate (prune) themselves based on information exchanged with neighbors.

Model the following behavior and requirements:
- Initially all processors are active. In each phase, processors may exchange messages carrying identifiers, proposals, or votes with their neighbors and update local state accordingly. Communication is unreliable only in timing (asynchronous): messages are delivered eventually and in FIFO order per edge (unless an explicit weaker assumption is chosen); no message corruption.
- A processor may decide to deactivate only when it has sufficient evidence that doing so will not disconnect the remaining active processors from each other with respect to the intended spanning structure (for example, preserving reachability between specific roots or maintaining a connected spanning backbone).
- The protocol must guarantee safety: at all times, the set of active processors induces a connected subgraph that satisfies the target connectivity invariant (e.g., contains a path between every pair of designated terminals, or remains connected overall).
- It must guarantee liveness: if communication continues and processors follow the protocol, the system converges in a finite number of phases to a stable configuration where no further deactivations occur.
- Specify progress fairness assumptions needed for termination and precise conditions under which processors may change state or send messages.
- Include correctness properties: eventual termination, preservation of required connectivity, and absence of simultaneous conflicting deactivations that could violate safety.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies the Yo-Yo leader-election algorithm with pruning on undirected, loop-free, connected graphs over a fixed set of numbered nodes. The initial state nondeterministically chooses a connected graph over Nodes, orients each edge from the smaller endpoint to the larger one, and then models the algorithm as alternating down and up phases in which nodes exchange messages, reverse edges, prune edges, and eventually deactivate non-leader nodes. The specification includes typing and structural invariants, a liveness property stating eventual termination, and a characterization of termination as exactly the deadlock states under weak fairness of Next.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies the Yo-Yo leader-election algorithm with pruning, verified over all undirected, loop-free, connected graphs on a fixed number of nodes `N`. Unlike a companion module that fixes a particular graph, the `Init` predicate existentially quantifies over all strongly connected subsets of the complete edge set, so model checking explores every possible initial topology.

Each node maintains Boolean `active` status, a current `phase` ("down" or "up"), sets of `incoming` and `outgoing` neighbors (establishing an initial orientation by node identity: lower-numbered nodes point to higher-numbered ones), and a `mailbox` of pending messages. The algorithm alternates between a down phase, in which nodes propagate the minimum identity received from upstream, and an up phase, in which nodes send "yes"/"no" replies back to their incoming neighbors and selectively prune or reverse edges. Sources initiate the down phase immediately; internal nodes and sinks wait until all expected down messages have arrived. During the up phase, edges carrying "no" replies are reversed, pruned edges are removed, and lone sinks deactivate themselves. The next-state relation allows any enabled node to execute either its down or up action, and weak fairness ensures every continuously enabled action is eventually taken.

The specification checks four properties: `TypeOK` (structural well-formedness of all variables), `NeighborInv` (consistency of incoming/outgoing sets across nodes, accounting for in-flight reversal or pruning messages), `FinishIffTerminated` (deadlock occurs exactly when the termination condition holds), and the liveness property `Liveness`, asserting that the algorithm eventually reaches a state where the minimum-identity node is the sole leader, all other nodes are inactive, and all mailboxes are empty.
desc_intent: Specify the Yo-Yo leader election algorithm with pruning, verified over all connected undirected loop-free graphs on a fixed number of nodes N. Initially, each node's edges are oriented by numeric order (lower-numbered node is incoming, higher-numbered is outgoing), and the topology is chosen nondeterministically from all connected subgraphs. Nodes alternate between a down phase, in which they propagate the minimum identifier received toward their outgoing neighbors, and an up phase, in which they reply yes or no and optionally request pruning of edges, progressively eliminating non-minimum sources and redirecting or removing edges until a single leader remains. The algorithm must satisfy the following properties: a type-correctness invariant; a neighbor consistency invariant ensuring that the outgoing/incoming relationship between any two nodes is coherent except when a reversal or pruning message is in transit; a termination condition stating that the algorithm finishes if and only if the node with the globally smallest identifier is the sole leader, all other nodes are inactive, and all mailboxes are empty; and a liveness property guaranteeing that this terminated state is eventually reached under weak fairness of all node actions.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a TLC-oriented wrapper around an atomic commit protocol specification, extending ACP_NB and adding a few top-level properties and a concrete postcondition witness. It defines a symmetry-related permutation operator, a reformulated temporal property AC4_alt about decision stability for participants, an eventual-commit property AllMustCommit, and a large PostCondition value that encodes a specific counterexample trace and visited states. The file does not define the underlying transition system itself; instead, it refers to state imported from the extended module and packages TLC data structures for checking or replaying a counterexample scenario involving two participants p0 and p1, coordinator failure, and participant crashes.
desc_intent: Specify a formal model of a synchronous atomic commit protocol for a fixed set of distributed participants (cohorts) that must reach a consistent global decision: either all participants that decide commit must stay committed forever, and all participants that decide abort must stay aborted forever. The system should model asynchronous steps of participants communicating with a coordinator (or running a coordinatorless consensus) and permit retries, message reordering, and failures of participants and the coordinator, subject to eventual reliable recovery or timeouts. The model should allow nondeterministic choices for initial participant states and for message delivery ordering, but must capture safety constraints that no participant can switch from commit to abort or from abort to commit once a final decision has been reached for that participant. It should express liveness expectations under reasonable fairness: if a sufficient set of non-faulty participants and the coordinator remain responsive, then a unanimous decision (commit or abort) is eventually reached by all non-faulty participants. Include invariants capturing validity (no participant can commit unless a prepare/accept condition was satisfied), agreement (no two non-faulty participants decide differently), and decision permanence (decisions are stable thereafter). Do not prescribe a particular algorithmic structure; focus on the protocol goals, fault model, permitted actions, and the safety and liveness properties to be verified.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a TLC-oriented wrapper around the ACP_SB specification, extending the underlying protocol module and TLC. It defines a symmetry-related helper operator using permutations of the participants, and rewrites the AC4 property into an explicit stuttering-invariant temporal formula over the participant variable. It also states a liveness-style property requiring that every participant eventually reaches either the commit or abort decision state.
desc_intent: Specify a formal TLA+ model of a fault-tolerant atomic commit protocol for a fixed set of participants coordinated by a coordinator. The model should capture messages exchanged (prepare, vote, commit, abort, and coordinator decisions), participant state transitions (initial, prepared, committed, aborted), and possible failures including coordinator crash and participant crash and recovery. The protocol must guarantee safety properties: agreement (no two non-faulty participants decide differently), validity (if any participant votes to abort then the final outcome is abort; if all vote to commit then the final outcome can be commit), and integrity (once a participant decides commit or abort it never reverts). Liveness should be stated as a weak guarantee under fair delivery and a bounded failure model: if the coordinator does not crash permanently and all non-faulty participants respond, then the protocol eventually reaches a decision. Model nondeterministic scheduling and message loss/duplication but allow assumptions (e.g., reliable retransmission or eventual delivery) needed for the liveness claim. Include symmetry reduction considerations for identical participants to keep state-space manageable. Specify invariants to prove and temporal properties to check with TLC, without prescribing the algorithmic steps for participants or coordinator.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module provides Apalache type annotations for another specification, ACP_SB, by declaring typed constants and variables and then instantiating the underlying module. The comments explain that the purpose is to keep the original specification free of tool-specific annotations while supplying concrete typing information for participants, participant state, coordinator state, and several tag constants such as yes, no, commit, and abort. The file itself does not define the protocol behavior, actions, or temporal properties; instead, it introduces the typed interface and a concrete set value for participants used by configuration.
desc_intent:
Specify a formal model of a two-phase commit (2PC) protocol with a single coordinator and a fixed set of participants. The model should capture asynchronous message delivery (messages may be delayed or lost), participant failures and recovery semantics, and non-Byzantine faults (processes may crash and later recover, but do not act maliciously). The system must support a prepare phase where the coordinator requests each participant’s vote (yes/no/undecided) and a commit/abort phase where the coordinator broadcasts the global decision (commit/abort) to all participants.

Require that the protocol guarantees: (1) Agreement — no two non-faulty participants decide differently (no split brain); (2) Atomicity — if any participant decides commit, then every participant that eventually decides must decide commit; (3) Validity — if all non-faulty participants vote yes and the coordinator does not crash permanently, the final decision is commit; conversely, if any non-faulty participant votes no, the decision is abort; (4) Termination under weak liveness assumptions — if messages are eventually delivered and crashed processes eventually recover, then all non-faulty participants eventually reach a decision; and (5) Coordinator consistency — the coordinator’s decision is consistent with the votes it received.

Model message channels abstractly (per-recipient queues or unreliable broadcast), allow explicit modeling of “vote sent/received” and “decision received/applied,” and expose participant and coordinator crash/recovery events. Specify invariants capturing safety properties and liveness properties expressed under fairness assumptions.

desc_declarative_gpt: This specification models a resource allocator that manages a finite set of resources for a set of clients, with explicit communication between clients and the allocator through a network of in-transit messages. Clients can issue requests only when they have no pending requests and hold no resources, allocations may satisfy requests only partially, and clients may return held resources even before their full request has been satisfied. The spec combines allocator state imported through an instance of a scheduling allocator with client-local state and message passing, and it verifies type correctness, a lower-level invariant relating allocator and client views, mutual exclusion of held resources, liveness of returns and eventual acquisition, and a recurring satisfaction property under weak fairness assumptions.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies a resource-allocation system in which a set of clients request, hold, and return shared resources managed by a central allocator. It extends an underlying `SchedulingAllocator` module and adds explicit client-side state and an asynchronous message-passing network between clients and the allocator.

The state consists of allocator variables (`unsat`, `alloc`, `sched`) tracking outstanding requests, current allocations, and a scheduling sequence, plus client variables (`requests`, `holding`) tracking each client's pending request and currently held resources, and a `network` set carrying messages of types `request`, `allocate`, and `return`. Initially all sets are empty. Clients send `Request` messages when they hold nothing and have no pending requests; the allocator processes these via `RReq`, then schedules clients via `Schedule`, and issues `Allocate` actions (following schedule order) that send `allocate` messages; clients receive these via `RAlloc`, updating `holding` and `requests`. Clients may return resources early via `Return`, which sends a `return` message processed by the allocator via `RRet`. Liveness is enforced by weak fairness on all message-reception actions, on `Schedule`, on allocations, and on clients returning resources once fully satisfied.

Safety properties verified include a type invariant, mutual exclusion over held resources (`ResourceMutex`), and a detailed structural invariant relating in-transit messages to the allocator's and clients' local state. Liveness properties assert that clients eventually obtain requested resources, eventually return them, and are satisfied infinitely often. The module also asserts that this specification is a refinement of the scheduling allocator abstraction.
desc_intent: Write a TLA+ specification for a resource allocator that manages a shared pool of resources among multiple clients, communicating via an asynchronous message-passing network. Clients may request a non-empty set of resources only when they hold nothing and have no pending requests; the allocator responds by allocating subsets of available resources, possibly incrementally; and clients may return resources they hold at any time, even before their full request is satisfied, though they are only obligated to return everything once fully satisfied. The allocator maintains a schedule of pending clients and allocates resources in schedule order, ensuring no client earlier in the schedule is denied a resource given to a later one. Messages of three kinds — request, allocate, return — travel through an unordered network and must eventually be delivered. The specification must guarantee mutual exclusion (no resource held by two clients simultaneously), that every client request is eventually fully satisfied, that clients who receive all requested resources eventually return them, and that every client is satisfied infinitely often. Liveness relies on fair message delivery, fair scheduling, fair allocation, and clients faithfully returning resources once their request is complete.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module states a refinement relationship between two allocator specifications. It extends SchedulingAllocator, instantiates SimpleAllocator as Simple, defines SimpleAllocator as Simple!SimpleAllocator, and asserts the theorem Allocator => SimpleAllocator.
desc_intent: Specify a refinement relationship between two resource-allocation systems: a high-level simple allocator and a lower-level scheduling allocator implementation. The model should describe requests from clients for exclusive access to a finite set of identical resources (or slots), how requests are granted and released, and how the scheduler maps requests onto resources over time. The simple allocator must be characterized by its abstract behavior: clients can request and later release resources, at most one client holds a given resource at a time, and every granted allocation corresponds to a previously issued request. The scheduling allocator must implement the same externally observable behavior while possibly using additional internal scheduling steps, queues, or preemption decisions. Require that every trace of the scheduling allocator, when observed only in terms of client requests, grants, and releases, is a valid trace of the simple allocator (refinement / trace inclusion). Safety properties: mutual exclusion on resources, no allocation without request, and invariant preservation of resource counts. Liveness properties: every pending request is eventually either granted or explicitly refused according to policy, and resources are eventually released if clients complete. Specify the refinement relation between observable actions and require a formal proof obligation showing the implementation implies the specification.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a resource allocator for a finite set of clients and resources. Clients issue resource requests only when they have no outstanding unsatisfied request and currently hold no resources; requests may be partially satisfied, resources may be returned early, and a schedule sequence constrains which client requests may be served before others. The specification includes weak fairness assumptions requiring clients to return resources once fully satisfied, requiring allocations to eventually happen when enabled, and requiring scheduling to eventually occur; it states and checks type, mutual exclusion, allocator invariants, and several liveness properties such as eventual return, eventual obtainment of requested resources, and infinitely often satisfied requests.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies a scheduling-based resource allocator that manages a shared pool of resources among a set of competing clients. Three variables track the system state: `unsat`, mapping each client to its current set of outstanding (unsatisfied) resource requests; `alloc`, mapping each client to the resources currently allocated to it; and `sched`, a sequence of clients representing the current allocation schedule.

Four actions define the next-state relation. `Request` allows a client with no pending requests and no held resources to submit a new non-empty resource request. `Schedule` non-deterministically appends a permutation of all currently unscheduled clients with pending requests to the end of the schedule sequence. `Allocate` grants a subset of available, requested resources to a client that appears in the schedule, provided no client appearing earlier in the schedule has requested any of those resources; when a client's request is fully satisfied it is removed from the schedule. `Return` allows a client to release any subset of its held resources at any time, even before its full request is met, though clients are only obligated to return resources once fully satisfied.

Liveness conditions require weak fairness of full returns when a client's request is satisfied, weak fairness of any partial allocation for each client, and weak fairness of scheduling. The module asserts six theorems: type correctness, mutual exclusion of allocated resources, a structural allocator invariant ensuring schedulability, and three liveness properties — that clients eventually return all resources, that every requested resource is eventually allocated, and that every client is infinitely often fully satisfied. The model-checking configuration instantiates three clients and two resources and checks all invariants and liveness properties.
desc_intent:
Specify a resource allocator that manages a finite set of resources among a set of competing clients using a scheduling discipline. Clients may request a non-empty set of resources only when all prior requests have been fulfilled and they hold no resources. Requests may be partially satisfied incrementally, and clients may return resources before their full request is met, but are only obligated to return resources once their entire request has been granted. The allocator maintains an ordered schedule of clients with outstanding requests; resources may be allocated to any scheduled client out of order, provided no client appearing earlier in the schedule has requested those resources. The schedule is extended by appending permutations of currently unscheduled clients with pending requests.

The specification must guarantee the following safety properties: resources are allocated exclusively (no resource held by two clients simultaneously), all clients in the schedule have outstanding requests, and the allocator can always satisfy each scheduled client's request assuming earlier-scheduled clients eventually release their resources. For liveness, assuming the allocator eventually schedules pending clients, eventually allocates available resources, and clients eventually return all held resources once fully satisfied, every client must obtain each requested resource eventually, every satisfied client must eventually release all resources, and every client must be fully satisfied infinitely often.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a simple resource allocator for a finite set of resources and a set of clients. Clients issue requests only when they currently hold no resources and have no outstanding unsatisfied request; requests may then be partially fulfilled over time, and clients may return held resources even before a request is completely satisfied. The specification defines two temporal system specifications with different fairness assumptions, and proves safety and liveness properties such as type correctness, mutual exclusion of resource ownership, eventual return, eventual obtainment, and infinitely often having no unsatisfied requests; it also includes a symmetry expression and a concrete counterexample value structure.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies a resource allocator managing a finite set of shared resources among a set of clients. Each client tracks two pieces of state: `unsat`, the set of resources it has outstanding requests for, and `alloc`, the set of resources currently allocated to it. Initially both mappings are empty for every client.

Three actions drive the system. `Request(c,S)` allows client `c` to submit a new request for a nonempty set `S`, but only when it holds no resources and has no pending unsatisfied request. `Allocate(c,S)` lets the allocator grant any nonempty subset of the available (unallocated) resources that overlap the client's outstanding request, partially fulfilling the request if needed. `Return(c,S)` allows a client to return any nonempty subset of its currently held resources, even before its full request has been satisfied.

The principal specification `SimpleAllocator` combines the initial condition and stuttering-closed next-state relation with weak fairness on full returns and strong fairness on allocations. A weaker variant, `SimpleAllocator2`, relaxes the return fairness condition to require returns only after the entire request has been satisfied. The model checks two invariants—`TypeInvariant` and `ResourceMutex` (no two clients hold the same resource simultaneously)—and three liveness properties: `ClientsWillReturn` (clients eventually release resources once satisfied), `ClientsWillObtain` (every requested resource is eventually allocated), and `InfOftenSatisfied` (every client is satisfied infinitely often). The theorems note that the weaker `SimpleAllocator2` preserves `ClientsWillReturn` but not the stronger liveness properties. The model is configured with three clients and two resources.
desc_intent:
Specify a resource allocator managing a shared pool of resources among a fixed set of clients. A client may submit a request for a nonempty set of resources only when it has no outstanding unsatisfied requests and currently holds no resources. The allocator may fulfill a request partially — allocating any nonempty subset of the requested resources that are currently available — and a client may return any subset of its held resources at any time, even before its full request has been satisfied. A client is only obligated to return resources once its entire request has been fulfilled.

The specification must guarantee the following properties: mutual exclusion (no resource is ever held by more than one client simultaneously); eventual return (whenever a client has no outstanding requests, it will eventually release all held resources); eventual allocation (every resource in an outstanding request will eventually be allocated to that client); and infinite satisfiability (every client's outstanding request is eventually fully satisfied infinitely often). Fairness conditions should ensure that allocations are made with strong fairness and that clients return their full allocation with weak fairness once fully satisfied.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module is a lightweight wrapper around another specification, intended to provide Apalache type annotations for a barrier specification instantiated from the module Barrier. It declares a constant N and a variable pc, and locally redefines the tuple vars as << pc >> in order to disambiguate the type of the 1-tuple used by the instantiated specification. The file itself contains no transition relation, temporal specification, or proof obligations; its main design purpose is to attach tool-specific typing information while leaving the original Barrier module unchanged.
desc_intent:
Specify a TLA+ model of a reusable barrier synchronization primitive for N concurrent processes. The model should treat N as a parameter and represent arbitrary process identities. Each process repeatedly executes phases where it performs local work, then waits at the barrier, and only proceeds past the barrier when all N processes have arrived. The barrier must be reusable: after all processes pass, they may start a new phase and synchronize again without interference from previous phases.

The model must capture asynchronous interleaving of steps, possible process speeds, and the fact that processes may repeatedly reach the barrier an unbounded number of times. It must not rely on shared-clock assumptions. Represent process-local states (e.g., working, waiting, released) and any shared control needed to enforce the barrier semantics.

Specify safety properties: (1) No process may be released from a barrier until all N processes have reached that same barrier instance (no premature release). (2) No process can be released for one barrier instance based on arrivals of a different instance (no cross-instance mixing). Specify liveness properties: eventually all processes that enter the barrier are released (no deadlock or permanent starvation), assuming fair scheduling of processes. Also include a property ensuring eventual reuse: after a complete release, processes can enter and be released by a subsequent barrier instance. Include parameters and invariants needed to reason about counts of arrivals and phase numbers, but do not fix an implementation strategy.

desc_declarative_gpt: This module specifies a simple reusable barrier synchronization protocol for N processes. Each process starts in control state "b0" and may individually move to "b1"; once all processes are in "b1", the barrier resets all processes back to "b0" simultaneously. The specification defines the initial state, the next-state relation, a type correctness condition for the program counter function, and a temporal barrier property stating that a process cannot leave the barrier while some other process has not yet entered it.
desc_declarative_claude:
The module specifies a cyclic barrier synchronization primitive for N processes. Each process is identified by an integer in the set 1..N, and the single variable `pc` maps each process to one of two program-counter locations, `"b0"` or `"b1"`.

Initially, all processes are at `"b0"`. The action `b0(self)` models an individual process arriving at the barrier: it advances that process's counter from `"b0"` to `"b1"` independently of all others. The action `b1` models the barrier release: it fires only when every process has reached `"b1"`, at which point all processes are simultaneously reset to `"b0"`, allowing the cycle to repeat. The temporal specification is a standard safety specification with no fairness constraints.

Two properties are checked with N set to 6. `TypeOK` is a type invariant confirming that `pc` always maps every process to one of the two valid locations. `BarrierProperty` is a state-machine safety property asserting that no process already past the barrier (at `"b1"`) can leave that state while any other process is still approaching it (at `"b0"`); formally, whenever some process is at `"b0"` and another is at `"b1"`, the latter must remain at `"b1"` in the next step.
